title: Prediction Markets Are Calling It Early
excerpt: This is an edition of Over/Under, a newsletter on the latest in prediction markets, gambling, and the evolution of everyday risk
body: This is an edition of Over/Under, a newsletter on the latest in prediction markets, gambling, and the evolution of everyday risk
Democrats aren’t the only ones celebrating this week
Prediction markets—high-speed betting arenas where users can wager on the future of the republic—have been claiming a win of their own
The platforms foresaw a Democratic sweep, and that’s what they got. “BREAKING: Polymarket was right,” one post on the company’s X account read yesterday morning
Both Polymarket and Kalshi have said that across the entire slate of elections that were called by Wednesday morning, about 98 percent of the markets’ favored candidates won
In many cases, prediction markets were able to identify the winners early and decisively
In Texas, Kalshi and Polymarket gave James Talarico about a 75 percent chance of victory in the days leading up to the election; he won
In Kansas, Adam Hamilton’s chances were hovering around 64 percent; he won too

Even before the major networks began to make their official calls Tuesday night, and before The New York Times ’ needle made its biggest swings, some of the probabilities on these platforms had approached 99 percent, indicating near-complete certainty about who the winners would be

Part of the original idea behind prediction markets was that they’d be able to draw on the wisdom of the crowd—millions and millions of individual hunches—to produce more accurate forecasts than any single source
The question after Tuesday’s elections is whether they can consistently align on outcomes that the polls and forecasts don’t see coming
Are prediction markets oracles or aggregators? So far, the evidence can’t justify the kind of grand victory they’re claiming
Not all of the markets’ favorites won their election; Democrats were often underestimated, just as they were in the polls
Many bettors failed to predict Darline Graham’s loss in South Carolina and Greg Abbott’s loss in Texas
And in some cases, the markets were jittery: Probabilities wavered up and down at the last minute in Texas , Arizona , and New York for unknown reasons
The markets proved themselves most useful this week when they could fill an information gap

The markets can be a rough index of public sentiment on Election Night, when the exit polls are out but the race still hasn’t been called—or in the days after when votes are still being counted, as in Alaska and Mississippi

As Bloomberg ’s Matt Levine put it yesterday: “It would be nice if someone else would piece everything together, weight it appropriately by how much it matters, and generate one simple answer to the question ‘who won?’” This is essentially what prediction markets have tried to do
But, Levine notes, the markets are largely piecing together information that already exists

Bettors can theoretically get their data from anywhere; they might make wagers based on polling, late-night cable-news broadcasts, their own surveys , or other reputable forecasts by experts such as Nate Silver (a paid adviser to Polymarket) and Lakshya Jain of Split Ticket

And at least on Polymarket, a small share of traders are handling the majority of the money—1 percent of accounts control 75 percent of the total volume, per the Anti-Corruption Data Collective , a nonprofit
That’s part of why the demographic makeup amd political biases of the people actually using these websites doesn’t skew the probabilities all that much
The especially active traders tend to bet according to who they think will win, rather than who they personally want to win
In many cases, the markets favored eventual winners about as much as the forecasting models did
Take New Hampshire’s Senate race: The day before the elections, Nate Silver’s FLIPR Deluxe and Split Ticket both gave the Democratic candidate, who eventually won, a 95 percent chance
At the same time, Kalshi and Polymarket had him at 94 and 95 percent, respectively
Were markets just putting their trust in Split Ticket and Silver? It’s possible, but the markets and the models are not always aligned

In the Nevada governor’s race, where the Democrat also beat his Republican opponent, VoteHub, another model, gave the Democrat a 58 percent chance of winning, and FLIPR Deluxe gave him a 53 percent chance
Kalshi and Polymarket had him at about 75 percent

This time, maybe the markets were more attuned to early voting, as Silver himself suggested —or maybe they just got lucky. (In many cases, overindexing on early voting is ill-advised.) The prediction-market industry had a lot to lose in these midterms—not only because lawmakers of both parties are preparing for a regulatory crackdown , but also because Tuesday night was a test of what these platforms can actually do
Kalshi and Polymarket have been trying to convince regulators and the American public that their markets have real uses for society beyond speculation
The industry’s position is that its platforms are public tools that can benefit observers just as much as the hedge funds and market makers who trade on them
But whether the markets can prove their worth as forecasters will depend on whether they can consistently produce the kind of discrepancy we saw in Nevada
For many commentators , this Tuesday was a testament to the power of these markets to forecast elections
In declaring victory, though, Kalshi and Polymarket are exaggerating the extent of their vindication
Despite the outsize media attention and PR, election markets represent a tiny fraction of today’s betting industry

Bloomberg reports that “last month, politics accounted for just 1% of trading volume across Kalshi and Polymarket, down from two-thirds during the 2024 presidential election.” Sports, parlays, and crypto trades make up the majority of that volume—and the majority of the revenue
It might be more accurate to say that these firms are sports-betting platforms with a politics function tacked on
Outside of elections, the social benefits of these markets are harder to see
Possible Futures In every edition, I’ll share my thoughts on a few news stories I’m watching

    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770374/original/file-20261105-78-cuap8a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5160%2C3440&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Iranians at a pro-regime rally in Tehran&#39;s Enqelab Square on Nov. 4, 2026, taunt U.S. President Donald Trump and his deputy, JD Vance.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/man-holds-the-portraits-of-irans-late-founder-of-the-news-photo/2303043308?phrase=Iran%20Vance&amp;adppopup=true">Atta Kenare/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>While votes were still being counted <a href="https://theconversation.com/epic-blue-wave-helps-democrats-take-congress-in-overwhelming-rebuke-to-president-trump-295830">in the U.S. midterm elections</a>, administration figures in Washington were already inviting speculation over how the results might be <a href="https://theconversation.com/with-control-of-congress-heres-how-democrats-could-stop-trumps-war-in-iran-295954">connected to the conflict with Iran</a>.</p>

<p>On the morning after the election, Vice President JD Vance <a href="https://x.com/JDVance/status/2118004988433641835">wrote on X</a> that the major reason for the dramatic loss for Republicans was the American public’s opposition to the war. “Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” he wrote, in reference to the ongoing conflict that began with U.S.-Israeli airstrikes against Iran in late February 2026.</p>

<p>While it is rare for a vice president to make such a critical proclamation about their own administration’s policy, President Donald Trump later stated that <a href="https://www.the-sun.com/news/17256408/jd-vance-blames-midterm-elections-loss-iran-war-trump/">he did not disagree with Vance’s appraisal</a> of the role that frustration with the Iran war played in voters’ minds.</p>

<p>But whether this changes Trump’s view on next steps in the ongoing conflict remains unclear. Reporting over the past few weeks has indicated that the U.S. military has been actively preparing options and <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/us/politics/us-israel-renewed-iran-strikes.html">increasing capabilities in the Persian Gulf region</a> in the event the president directs a resumption of hostilities.</p>

<p>As an <a href="https://fordschool.umich.edu/faculty/javed-ali">expert on Middle East affairs</a> and a former senior official at the National Security Council during the first Trump administration, I’m aware that months of conflict have failed to bring Iran to its knees, force regime change or militarily defeat a perceived threat to U.S. assets and allies. Escalating now is unlikely to change those realities – and it carries the additional risk of further damaging Republicans in the eyes of Americans voters as they turn toward the 2028 presidential race.</p>

<p>Even if Trump were to ratchet up the conflict, moreover, it’s unclear how much wiggle room he’ll have come January facing a Democratic Congress almost <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/04/politics/video/jeffries-says-ending-iran-war-will-be-top-of-house-democrats-agenda">uniformly opposed to the war</a>.</p>

<h2>Sunk costs</h2>

<p>Part of the issue facing Iran war hawks in Washington now is that the conflict has caused serious setbacks for the regime in Tehran without satisfying the officially stated strategic reasons for going to war.</p>

<p>They argue that pulling back now – as welcome as that might be for Americans struggling with the associated rising cost of fuel – may allow Iran to rebuild before the conflict is “won.” Moreover, it would render the military and reputational costs already sunk by Washington as wasted.</p>

<p>Among the achievements of this war touted by the Trump administration has been the <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/02/28/middleeast/ayatollah-khamenei-iran-killed-airstrike-intl-latam">death of former Supreme Leader Ali Khameini</a>, along with the killing of scores of <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/israel-says-irgc-navy-commander-killed-iranian-top-envoy-said-removed-from-hit-list/">senior leaders within the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps</a> – including individuals like the <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/3/3/who-is-ali-larijani-the-iranian-official-promising-a-lesson-to-the-us">former head of Iran’s National Security Council Ali Larijani</a>. Significant elements of Iran’s air defense and radar network, <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/16/us-says-it-has-destroyed-iran-missile-capacity-how-is-iran-still-shooting">ballistic missile and drone production, and storage and launch sites</a> have also been destroyed. And Iran’s <a href="https://www.aerotime.aero/articles/iran-dwindling-air-force-can-jets-still-fly-drone-attacks">already outdated navy and air force</a> has been further degraded. </p>

<p>Meanwhile, the U.S.-imposed <a href="https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PUBLIC-RELEASES/Article/4542098/us-forces-to-resume-naval-blockade-against-iran/">naval blockade</a> against Iranian-linked shipping in the Persian Gulf cut off a crucial lifeline for Iran’s economy. And <a href="https://www.state.gov/iran-sanctions/">additional sanctions and economic penalties</a> imposed by Washington have served to <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/iran-currency-getting-obliterated-regime-214000456.html">further devalue Iran’s currency</a> and <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/14/how-do-iranians-move-money-abroad-to-avoid-us-sanctions">deprive Iran of additional financial links</a> to the international banking system.  </p>

<h2>Down but not out</h2>

<p>Yet for all the U.S. successes in degrading the Iranian military by limitless aerial bombardment and the significant financial pressure against the Iranian economy, an obvious endgame remains elusive.</p>

<p>Despite weakening the Iranian government – now led by Ali Khameinei’s son, Mojtaba, and a <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/06/05/middleeast/iran-supreme-leader-adviser-mohsen-rezaei-interview-intl">new echelon of senior IRGC commanders</a> – the Islamic Republic remains intact. Moreover, it <a href="https://www.jpost.com/middle-east/iran-news/article-911221">still possesses enough ballistic missiles and drones</a> to hold the region at risk, while continuing <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/25/irans-authorities-take-self-sacrifice-mobilisation-campaign-nationwide">to impose significant control over its population</a>. </p>

<p>Meanwhile, U.S. military spending continues to rise. In September, the U.S. Congressional Budget Office assessed that the <a href="https://www.cbo.gov/publication/62756">military costs of the Iran War had already totaled US$38 billion</a>. Since then, that <a href="https://www.militarytimes.com/news/2026/10/28/us-costs-of-iran-war-rise-to-over-47-billion-according-to-pentagon-estimate/">number has only increased</a>. And that is to say nothing of the associated global economic costs that have resulted from Iran’s de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz – a key shipping route for oil and gas.</p>

<p>Should Trump decide to change course on Iran, he – and others – may think that the money, effort and <a href="https://www.militarynews.com/news/national/families-of-some-us-troops-killed-in-the-iran-wars-deadliest-strike-absent-from-white/article_2ddea9b5-b98f-5f10-bd28-3a1b82aa2621.html">lives of 19 American servicemen</a> killed in the conflict would have been spent with no obvious objective achieved. Yet continued military expenditure with no strategic endgame could only magnify those same costs.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>To Iran, the midterm results have not changed its public position. Mojtaba Khameini has issued statements <a href="https://www.newsweek.com/khamenei-orders-iran-military-response-without-geographical-limitations-12644735">directing the IRGC to widen the conflict in the region and perhaps beyond</a> should the U.S. and Israel attack again. At the same time, <a href="https://www.usnews.com/news/world/articles/2026-11-04/irans-khamenei-says-us-hostility-will-persist-regardless-of-party-in-power">a statement attributed to him</a> indicates that hostilities between the United States and Iran will persist regardless of the balance of party political power in Washington. </p>

<p>This raises questions about <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/31/qatar-iran-us-talks-mediation.html">the prospects for diplomacy</a>. During the summer, the U.S. and Iran agreed to an <a href="https://arabcenterdc.org/resource/memorandum-of-understanding-between-the-united-states-of-america-and-the-islamic-republic-of-iran/">initial 14-point memorandum of understanding</a> that, if finalized, could have brought a permanent end to the hostilities. But since the <a href="https://arabcenterdc.org/resource/memorandum-of-understanding-between-the-united-states-of-america-and-the-islamic-republic-of-iran/">60-day clock on that agreement lapsed</a>, no parallel diplomatic agreement has emerged.</p>

<h2>No practical solution</h2>

<p>Even with the major shift in the U.S. political landscape, it remains unclear whether Trump will resume operations against Iran before the new Congress is sworn in. The messy election result in Israel – which has left the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-pressured-israel-military-attack-iran-runup-to-election">pro-war, and potentially outgoing, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyanu</a> with potentially more reason to double-down in Iran – only complicates matters.</p>

<p>The U.S. military certainly appears to be ready to engage in a new round of attacks against Iran if so directed, and Iran is ready to retaliate. But given <a href="https://nypost.com/2026/09/15/us-news/iran-war-effort-hampered-by-munitions-shortfalls-production-bottlenecks-pentagon-watchdog-finds/">the shortcomings in the U.S. inventory</a> – with munitions and missile and air defense capabilities depleted by eight months of war – escalation is something Trump and his inner circle will have to consider with caution.</p>

<p>Iran might force the issue by engaging in <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/uk-raf-fairford-terror-plot-iran-2-men-charged-security-offenses/">asymmetric attacks</a> in the region or beyond that they have not attempted already. Or it could launch a coordinated offensive with its partners in the region – notably the Houthis in Yemen, who have become more active <a href="https://time.com/article/2026/10/15/who-are-the-houthi-rebels-saudi-arabia-oil-airport-attacks/">in their own conflict with Saudi Arabia</a> in recent months.</p>

<p>But save an event that the Trump administration perceives is giving it cover to act, there are no clear indications emerging from Washington as to which way it will move.</p>

<p>Vance diagnosed a widely perceived political problem for Republicans: Voters don’t want more war. But what he noticeably didn’t mention was a practical solution. The Middle East conflict – and the United States’ role in it – are, as such, locked in a stalemate. </p>

<p>America and Iran have both borne significant political, military and economic costs. A decision not to pursue an endgame would leave those sunk; doing so may only increase them.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295938/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Should Trump decide to change course on Iran, he – and others – may think that the money, effort and lives of 19 American servicemen killed in the conflict would have been spent with no obvious objective achieved
Yet continued military expenditure with no strategic endgame could only magnify those same costs
Angel Rampersad – one of 19 U.S. service members killed in the Iran war
Spencer Platt/Getty Images To Iran, the midterm results have not changed its public position
Mojtaba Khameini has issued statements directing the IRGC to widen the conflict in the region and perhaps beyond should the U.S. and Israel attack again
At the same time, a statement attributed to him indicates that hostilities between the United States and Iran will persist regardless of the balance of party political power in Washington
This raises questions about the prospects for diplomacy
During the summer, the U.S. and Iran agreed to an initial 14-point memorandum of understanding that, if finalized, could have brought a permanent end to the hostilities
But since the 60-day clock on that agreement lapsed , no parallel diplomatic agreement has emerged
No practical solution Even with the major shift in the U.S. political landscape, it remains unclear whether Trump will resume operations against Iran before the new Congress is sworn in

The messy election result in Israel – which has left the pro-war, and potentially outgoing, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyanu with potentially more reason to double-down in Iran – only complicates matters
The U.S. military certainly appears to be ready to engage in a new round of attacks against Iran if so directed, and Iran is ready to retaliate

But given the shortcomings in the U.S. inventory – with munitions and missile and air defense capabilities depleted by eight months of war – escalation is something Trump and his inner circle will have to consider with caution
Iran might force the issue by engaging in asymmetric attacks in the region or beyond that they have not attempted already

title: The Speaker Who Gave the House Away
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture

Outgoing Speaker of the House Mike Johnson made a statement earlier this year that captured his approach to the job: “I have no intention of getting in the way of President Trump and his administration.” He was answering a question about levying tariffs, a power the Constitution gives to Congress
That’s been the pattern for most of Johnson’s tenure
When the interests of the White House and the House diverged, Johnson proved loyal to Trump and a traitor to the institution he was supposed to lead
As his run ends, I wonder: Has he been the worst speaker of all time? His partisan affiliations and views are not the deciding factors in this evaluation
If a speaker is to be judged by the legislation he helped to pass or the worst parts of his ideology or conduct, then each one who entrenched slavery would clearly rank lower

But if a speaker is to be judged on how he performs the core job of protecting the House’s independence and authority over its enumerated powers, then no speaker has done more than Johnson to subvert the constitutional and civic purpose of that vital institution
In 2016, Johnson, who practiced constitutional law, was elected to the House of Representatives after one term in the Louisiana state legislature
When Trump lost the 2020 election, Johnson helped organize and signed an amicus brief in a lawsuit that sought to overturn Joe Biden’s victories in Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin
Capitol, Johnson joined Republicans who wanted to overturn Biden’s wins in Arizona and Pennsylvania
That readiness to subordinate the will of American voters to Trump’s ambitions may have helped Johnson become speaker in 2023, and it foreshadowed his sycophancy after Trump’s return to office

The power of the purse is a key function of the House, yet Johnson sided with Trump, and against horrified fiscal conservatives, to pass a spending bill that violated his own standard of how to wield that power responsibly

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the most significant legislation that he engineered into law, is expected to increase deficits by trillions of dollars —despite Johnson’s own promise to resolve what he rightly describes as “unprecedented debt and spending” that jeopardize the country’s stability and security
Power over tariffs, declarations of war, and oversight of the executive branch are other core responsibilities of Congress

On tariffs, Johnson did not merely acquiesce as Trump usurped an Article I power to impose duties on foreign nations (a congressional authority that Johnson had once sought to protect before he became speaker)—he took steps to stymie the ability of fellow House members to cast votes against the president’s tariffs
This speaker has repeatedly acted to stop the House from speaking
When Trump launched a war against Iran, without congressional approval or public support, Johnson tried to shut down floor action to prevent a war-powers vote that would rebuke him
When House members attempted to force the release of files associated with the Jeffrey Epstein investigation in 2025, Johnson adjourned the session early , sending lawmakers home to delay a vote

After the Democrat Adelita Grijalva won a House seat in an Arizona special election that September, Johnson delayed swearing her in for 50 days , a dereliction of his duty to ensure that his fellow Americans were represented

Democrats accused him of stalling because her signature on the Epstein petition would have forced a vote. (Johnson denied that the Epstein matter influenced his decision, and later voted to disclose the files, after Trump changed his position on the release.) All the while, amid allegations of presidential corruption related to foreign gifts and investment, pardons and clemency , stock profiteering and suspicious no-bid federal contracts , Johnson’s House has all but abdicated its oversight role
For almost two years, Trump has been mostly unchecked
Only future oversight can clarify the full costs of that inattention
Admittedly, there is no definite way to identify the worst speaker in history
Since the first Congress, 56 individuals have presided over the House
Americans constantly rank past presidents against one another
Vanishingly few could name 10 speakers, let alone compare them
Even experts had seemingly never bothered to rank House speakers until 1998, when an Iowa State University master’s student named Dennis Roy Still sent a survey to 60 congressional scholars

Although he soon realized that many of them were “unfamiliar with the speakership prior to the Civil War,” he found that the worst-ranked speaker was William Pennington, an inexperienced and ineffectual leader who was elected in 1859, shortly before the Civil War

Among modern speakers, Jim Wright is remembered for resigning amid a slew of ethics-violations allegations, and highly partisan speakers such as Newt Gingrich and Nancy Pelosi have been regarded as especially effective or especially divisive—depending on whom you ask
Then there’s Denny Hastert, the speaker from 1999 to 2007, who is a clear villain: Long after his tenure as speaker, he admitted to sexually abusing children
But even judging him on his official acts alone, the Nation writer John Nichols declared in 2007 that Hastert was “the most lamentable” speaker in history

Bush, a fellow Republican, to invade Iraq and Afghanistan without declaring war and “rubber-stamped the administration’s anti-Constitutional assaults on civil liberties,” Nichols argued, rendering “an essential legislative chamber as nothing more than an extension of the executive branch.” Although I believe that Bush-era Congresses often voted unwisely, at least they did vote on matters including the Authorization for Use of Military Force in Afghanistan, the Patriot Act, and the Iraq War (Hastert helped introduce the 2002 authorization for force in Iraq)
Compare this with Johnson’s House, which never authorized the use of military force in Trump’s Venezuela war or his Iran war
Although a war-powers vote on Iran did eventually happen, it took place in spite of Johnson
And this undeclared war persists without House-imposed consequences for the president
Add in tariffs and oversight, and all told, the current House has abdicated its constitutional role far more than Hastert’s did
On Tuesday, voters gave their verdict on the House that Johnson led
In a historic rebuke, they ousted Republicans from power
Democrats, who currently hold four fewer House seats than Republicans, are projected to have at least a 50-seat majority in 2027
Beyond that decisive signal of disapproval from voters, Johnson’s legacy will be undermining the independence of the legislative branch

title: Democrats Have No Coherent Plan for AI
excerpt: Among the many gifts that Donald Trump bequeathed to Democrats ahead of the midterms was allowing them the exclusive political use of the AI backlash
body: Among the many gifts that Donald Trump bequeathed to Democrats ahead of the midterms was allowing them the exclusive political use of the AI backlash
Now that Democrats have decisively won control of Congress, voters will expect them to follow through on their rhetoric
The problem is that Democrats don’t actually have a plan to regulate AI
In fact, they don’t even agree on what problems need to be solved in the first place
Until recently, federal AI legislation seemed impossible until 2029 at the earliest
Trump has consistently opposed any form of AI regulation, going so far as to pressure Congress to preempt state laws
Although some Republican lawmakers have seemed more sympathetic to AI regulation, almost none would dare defy their party’s leader

Of the roughly 150 AI-focused bills that have been proposed during Trump’s second term, only one—a bill that criminalized the nonconsensual posting of sexual images, including AI-generated ones—ultimately passed
Tuesday night’s astonishing results have made AI regulation a much more realistic possibility
Democrats could easily pass an AI bill through the House of Representatives, where they will have a huge majority
And with their surprisingly large Senate majority, they would need only a handful of Republicans to get to a filibuster-proof 60 votes
Republicans could be far more likely to vote with Democrats on AI following an electoral shellacking in which voters made abundantly clear that Trump was on the wrong side of the issue
The threat of a veto remains, but as a lame duck, the president might not care as much as he used to about the risk of slowing down the AI-driven stock-market boom
So Democrats might be able to get something done about AI
They just don’t seem to know what that something should be
This is true even when it comes to the one AI-related issue that, politically speaking, most obviously needs to be addressed: data centers
Voters are overwhelmingly opposed to the construction of data centers in their communities

Several candidates, including James Talarico in Texas, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Sherrod Brown in Ohio, and Annie Andrews in South Carolina, placed their opposition to data centers at the core of their campaign
But opinions differ widely about what the precise problem with data centers is and what ought to be done about them
Some politicians focused on rising power bills and proposed making data centers pay for their own electricity generation and grid upgrades
Some seized on the fact that many data-center deals are done in secret, and argued that they should be subject to local approval
And others proposed getting rid of data-center tax breaks
A few candidates, such as Gina Hinojosa, now Texas’s governor-elect, and Andrews, campaigned on a full data-center moratoriums

These proposals varied widely in how long they would last and under what conditions they would be lifted. [ Matteo Wong: Silicon Valley’s very bad night ] Even if Democrats did agree on what to do about data centers, federal legislation wouldn’t necessarily be the right way to achieve their goals
Most Democrats have cast the issue as a state and local one
This might explain why Senator Bernie Sanders’s proposal for a federal data-center ban attracted zero co-sponsors in the Senate
Beyond data centers, the questions get harder still
For starters, the party doesn’t have one shared view of what aspects of AI need to be regulated
Some are worried about the possibility of mass job losses caused by automation, others about AI deepfakes or children becoming overly attached to chatbot companions
Considerable disagreement exists over how to address each of these concerns
Take “AI safety”—the set of fears that ranges from rogue AI agents carrying out cyberattacks to the possibility of superintelligent systems wiping out all of humanity
Many Democrats believe that something needs to be done to prevent AI from causing problems in the real world
But the ideas for how to do this are all over the place, and each has its own drawbacks
One school of thought focuses on making sure that AI companies can be held legally responsible if and when their models cause harm
But liability is a fix that occurs only after the damage has already been done

As Charlie Bullock, the senior policy director for the Institute for Law and AI, put it to me, “No one can sue if we’re all dead.” Another idea is to require companies to build a “kill switch” that would shut their models down at the federal government’s command
But knowing whether a model is acting in dangerous ways before the damage occurs is difficult

Earlier this year, a group of rogue AI agents hacked into the company Hugging Face as well as OpenAI’s own internal servers without anyone at the company, let alone anyone in the federal government, realizing what had happened until well after the attacks had occurred
In other words, by the time someone thinks to reach for the kill switch, it may be too late
Recently, bipartisan momentum has been building to require AI companies to submit to safety audits, managed by either a new federal agency or approved third-party organizations

title: The Ballad of Bob Dylan and the Pope
excerpt: At first, the image appears to be some kind of intergalactic photo op, something out of Star Wars
body: At first, the image appears to be some kind of intergalactic photo op, something out of Star Wars
A figure hooded in black, his craggy face partly in shadow, greets a serene-looking man in a white robe
Think Emperor Palpatine shaking hands with Obi-Wan Kenobi, perhaps brokering a cease-fire in the Clone Wars
Closer inspection yields a picture that is no less weird: Bob Dylan is hanging with the pope
What they actually spoke about during their meeting yesterday at the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace, we may never know

But the questions only begin there! Why is Dylan’s head covered by a hood? Why, in some photos, does he have gloves and an umbrella? Why does he seem to have abandoned tying his polka-dotted tie mid-flip? And: Is the pope a fan? (Actually, that last one might have an answer—in a recent book about disarmament, the pope quoted Dylan’s 1963 deep cut “Go Away You Bomb”; “I want that Bomb—I want it settin in my mouth like a cigar,” goes one line
This is unfiltered Dylan that only a true fan could love.) The most famous American musician of the past half century visits the leader of the Catholic Church
The strangeness, if not the Sith hood, makes you laugh
But these two make some sense together, if not as obvious friends then at least, each in their own way, as spiritually ambitious people
Robert Zimmerman, born in Duluth, Minnesota, in 1941, meet Robert Francis Prevost, born in Chicago in 1955
They share the common matter-of-factness of people who grew up on the flat plains, who were born in the middle
They even have similarly enigmatic smiles—lips tight in a straight line, not giving away too much
Their gifts to each other were pretty unfussy, too

Dylan handed the pope a copy of his memoir, Chronicles: Volume One , and the pope gave Dylan—of course—a rosary. [ Read: The pope doubles down on the beautiful struggle ] From their middle-class, conventional Middle American upbringings, they both embarked on wild transformations
Dylan used traditional American music to mold himself into a troubadour from nowhere
He abandoned his given name, invented a mythology around his origins, and still resists definition
Prevost had a different kind of reinvention
He joined an ancient religious order, submitted himself to its disciplines, and ultimately assumed an identity set by its history, losing his name to become the pope
Two midwestern-American boys, avatars of self-transformation, now aged but still happily wearing costumes

But there’s more: In a moment when so many people are worried about how artificial intelligence is flattening human expression, could there be anything more affirming of human uniqueness than the life and work of Dylan and the pope? Even Dylan’s idiosyncratic outfit was the product of ingenuity that a computer couldn’t dream of matching, if computers could dream

The workwear designer Gauthier Borsarello instantly spotted that the jacket was his own creation. “The good thing about designing everything (even the puller of your zipper) from scratch is recognizing your own design without a doubt,” Borsarello wrote on Instagram
The pope, meanwhile, has become one of the most eloquent defenders of human creativity in the face of technological advance

His encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas , published this year, articulated beautifully why human limitations and our efforts to overcome them make us special and give our lives meaning. “Authentic culture and art” preserve a “spark,” he wrote; they allow people to take in the experiences of others, all the vulnerability and pain, and reflect them back in ways that elevate, resulting in Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony and Picasso’s Guernica . (And why not “Subterranean Homesick Blues”?—though the pope sadly didn’t put this on his list of faves.) And then there’s Dylan

Perhaps no other artist has reveled for so long in mixing and matching as much as he does, ingesting enormous quantities of cultural material, breaking them into pieces, and recombining them into something new
That’s been his whole schtick, from the beginning

In a way it anticipates what AI has supercharged, but he does it as only a human can, informed by a lifetime of listening, reading, performing, and inhabiting the American cultural imagination. [ Read: Rock and roll faces the inevitable ] Take “A Hard Rain’s a-Gonna Fall,” from 1962

In it, he riffs on the question-and-answer structure from a traditional English-Scottish border ballad called “Lord Randall” (“Oh where ha’e ye been, Lord Randall, my son? O where ha’e ye been, my handsome young man?”)

But Dylan infuses the form with surreal, apocalyptic imagery related to the Cold War and the anxiety of annihilation: “And what did you hear, my blue-eyed son? And what did you hear, my darling young one? I heard the sound of a thunder, it roared out a warnin’
Heard the roar of a wave that could drown the whole world.” Only the synapses of his weird brain could produce this

In his 2001 album, Love and Theft (an aptly titled middle finger to anyone who has a problem with this method), he lifts whole sentences from Confessions of a Yakuza , the memoir of a Japanese gangster

I’d like to think this is the question Dylan and the pope, sitting next to bookcases full of Catholic exegesis, discussed: What makes humans worth preserving? The photo of them is indelible because it’s sort of the answer
They’re dressed in black and in white, the whole spectrum of good to evil
One’s an artist and the other’s a priest, each aspiring to prophecy

They’re both accessing something larger than themselves, even though when you look at them, they’re small, old men, nearer to the end of their existences than to the beginning—the pope battling cancer, and Dylan in his mid-80s

title: This Won’t Be Easy for Democrats
excerpt: James Talarico talked a lot during his campaign about the so-called wilderness—as in, the electoral wasteland and morale morass that Democrats had been languish
body: James Talarico talked a lot during his campaign about the so-called wilderness—as in, the electoral wasteland and morale morass that Democrats had been languishing in since President Trump’s reelection, in 2024
In Texas, this felt like something of a permanent condition
Talarico preferred a more sanguine interpretation of wilderness, something I’ve thought about after he became the first Texas Democrat to win a Senate race since 1988

The wilderness, he said from early on in his campaign, could in fact prove a fertile ground for reinvention. “There is an opportunity to redefine the Democratic Party,” Talarico told me. “And you can’t do that if the brand is super set, or if there’s a strong leader at the top of the party.” This was a little over a year ago, and we were sitting in the lobby bar of an Arlington, Texas, hotel. “The wilderness,” Talarico continued, “is where new ideas and new leaders and new movements come forth.” At the time, I was inclined to dismiss this as a rationalization from another one of those fool’s-gold Democratic hopefuls in Texas
In retrospect, maybe Talarico was onto something

If nothing else, the Democrats’ midterm rout of Trump and his supine coalition of Republicans would seem to put to rest, at least for now, the long-running discussion of Democrats as a party out of touch, ill-defined, lacking in purpose, and perpetually ambling in this “wilderness.” I admit that I participated in a fair amount in this Democratic-doldrums discourse myself, including in an opus about the party adrift that ran in February, which now feels like a decade ago

It was true then, and had been for nearly four years, if you start the clock with the 2022 midterms and the disastrous denouement of the Biden years. [ Read: Democrats will likely disappoint voters soon ] The sheer magnitude of Tuesday’s drubbing of Republicans should provide an antidote to the wallowing that Democrats can be prone to

It’s impossible not to see the geographic reach of their victories, the generational ascent of so many potential stars, and the stunning margins that Democrats ran up across the country and not conclude that the party has legitimate reason to feel good about itself
This was a bona fide “thumpin,’” as another unpopular Republican president, George W
Bush, called his own midterm debacle 20 years ago

The requisite chest-thumpin’ from Democrats commenced immediately on Tuesday night. “We have five words for the American people,” Chuck Schumer, the likely next Senate majority leader, proclaimed to reporters as the returns poured in. “Relief is on the way.” Here are five more words for Democrats to keep in mind: Enjoy this while it lasts
The “what next” of this discussion is now at hand

And it’s pretty clear that Democrats should avoid the obvious trap of thinking that their victory means they’ve magically solved their “brand problem,” “trust problem,” or “working-class-voter problem,” among various others

The initial sense of punch-drunk euphoria will yield to questions about what the party’s sprawling new legislative majorities should focus on, how they should engage (if at all) with Trump and Republicans, what ideological framework (progressive versus moderate) they should embrace, and who should lead them going into 2028
Political victory laps can be fun but fleeting, especially for governing tribes famously given to angst and discord
Inevitably, the second-guessing and hand-wringing will return, and probably soon
In politics, the simplest explanation for an election result is usually the smartest one (and less time-consuming than reading those endless postmortems)
Tuesday’s result can be overwhelmingly ascribed to a repudiation of Trump, rather than revealing anything definitive about the diverse assortment of Democrats who prevailed

The political analyst Charlie Cook, of The Cook Political Report, gave preliminary voice to this notion when he predicted in September that this midterm would represent a “red undertow” rather than a blue wave

The results would be driven more by revulsion toward Trump and his various legislative lickspittles than by any dramatic reinvention by Democrats—or by some sudden mass affection for them by the electorate

This was rendered vividly in an NBC News poll released just before the election, in which voters declared themselves just not that into Democrats, despite their massive advantages leading into Election Day
Only 29 percent of respondents said that they viewed the party favorably, while 38 percent viewed Republicans positively
About half of the people surveyed said that they held a negative view of both parties
Trump will be around as the Democrats’ go-to foil for only so much longer
He has been a turnout machine for them as well as for Republicans
He has defined the GOP for the past decade, and has also defined the Democrats in opposition

It is not hard to imagine that a Republican president who did not, say, capriciously impose tariffs, start unpopular wars, or talk incessantly about building a White House ballroom would have had a considerably better midterm experience than Trump and the GOP just did
And far fewer Americans would have ever heard of Senators-Elect Talarico, Annie Andrews (South Carolina), or Adam Hamilton (Kansas)
What should also be clear to Democrats is that their time is limited
Again and again, voters have shown punishing impatience with parties that don’t deliver for them quickly, especially on such close-to-the-bone economic issues as inflation
Americans have not hesitated to swing back and forth between the two parties

When was the last election, anyway, in which voters have not been described as “angry,” “frustrated,” or “fed-up?” [ Read: ‘We did this for this man?’ ] In the short term, at least, Democrats can break out their Nutter Butters and enjoy the crack-up on the other side, where the center of political drama and division in America has shifted decisively since Tuesday

House Speaker Mike Johnson said that he won’t run for minority leader, setting up a potentially bitter race to succeed him; Vice President Vance blamed Tuesday’s pummeling on the Iran war (wait, whose idea was that?); and Trump chalked up the defeat to not being on the ballot himself (effectively blaming Republicans who were)
Democrats suddenly have real leverage in Washington
Trump is, to say the least, not easily humbled and not much for self-examination or course correction (to wit, he spent part of yesterday showing off his in-progress White House ballroom)
He is, however, a survivor, and will take what lifelines are available
Lo and behold: “I have a lot of friends who are Democrats, believe it or not,” Trump said on Fox. “I’ve already spoken to some of them,” he added
Presumably, one of these people was Schumer , who indicated Tuesday that he would be open to working with Trump, so long as he “will actually change his ways.” It certainly beats the wilderness

Yesterday, I reached out to Democratic National Committee chair Ken Martin, whose arrival in Washington last year was marked by infighting at the DNC, a fundraising drought, and unflattering stories about him in the press—my own among them
I’d made him the hapless head of Democratic doom in my article in February, characterizing the chairman’s demeanor as one of “resting dread face,” a description that he presumably did not appreciate

title: The Execution Divide
excerpt: Today, California Governor Gavin Newsom announced that he will commute the sentences of every prisoner on the state’s death row—548 people in all
body: Today, California Governor Gavin Newsom announced that he will commute the sentences of every prisoner on the state’s death row—548 people in all

With this action, Newsom could effect the largest-ever reduction of America’s death-row population, dropping the national total by about 27 percent. (California’s supreme court must approve some of the clemency requests.) California last executed a prisoner in 2006, and in 2019 Newsom instituted a moratorium against the death penalty via executive order
But in both 2012 and 2016, Californians narrowly voted against ballot measures that would have repealed the state’s death penalty, meaning many in the state would still prefer to see it in use
Newsom’s commutation order could foreclose that possibility in at least the near future
Newsom’s commutations underscore how polarized the country has become on the death penalty

Although several states have rejected capital punishment in recent years, a handful of red states are pushing back against that trend, taking ever more extreme measures to hand down death sentences and carry out executions

America’s death-penalty landscape is defined by dueling philosophies, which means that prisoners convicted of capital crimes face radically different outcomes depending on minor changes in geography: The fate of the same person committing the same murder on either side of the border between Texas, where executions are relatively common, and New Mexico, which does not permit capital punishment, would come down to only a few miles

The death penalty in America could grow ever more arbitrary and cruel before it dissolves altogether. [ From the July 2025 issue: Inside America’s death chambers ] State executives across the country have undertaken commutation actions similar to Newsom’s in recent years

When Colorado’s legislature abolished the state’s death penalty in 2020, Governor Jared Polis commuted all remaining death sentences; likewise, Governor Kate Brown commuted the death sentences of everyone on Oregon’s death row in 2022
In 2024, North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper issued 15 death-row commutations, reducing the state’s death-row population by roughly 10 percent
That same year, President Biden commuted the death sentences of 37 prisoners, leaving only three still facing death at the hands of the federal government
As of 2023, Governor Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania has maintained a de facto moratorium on executions by issuing reprieves for every death warrant that comes across his desk
And earlier this year, Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, a moderate Republican, granted his first death-row commutation and publicly urged his state’s legislature to abolish capital punishment altogether
Newsom’s intervention could give this trend considerable momentum
This pattern is in some respects unsurprising

The death penalty has been in a long-term decline for decades: Support for capital punishment for murder dropped from 80 percent during the 1990s to somewhere between 52 percent and 66 percent currently, depending on the phrasing of polling questions. ( Pew has detected a slight uptick in recent years.) In 1986, 325 new death sentences were handed down by juries across the country; in 2025, juries sentenced fewer than 30 prisoners to die, thanks in part to declining crime rates, criminal-justice reform efforts, and wide publicization of death-row exonerations

In recent years, several states have legislatively abolished the death penalty: New Hampshire in 2019, Colorado in 2020, Virginia in 2021, Washington in 2023, and Delaware in 2024, bringing the number of abolitionist states to 23
And the death penalty’s prospects going forward are dimming; younger generations are less likely to support it than their predecessors

America seems closer than ever to joining 74 percent of countries globally that have abandoned the death penalty—almost, but not quite. [ Elizabeth Bruenig: Donald Trump dreams of more executions ] Use of the death penalty today is concentrated in a handful of traditionally red states, among them Texas, Florida, Oklahoma, Alabama, and Missouri, which together carried out roughly 68 percent of the country’s executions in 2025

Florida in particular has undergone a death-penalty renaissance in recent years, ratcheting up annual executions over the past two years, no longer requiring juries to hand down death sentences unanimously, and permitting the use of capital punishment to include non-homicide offenses such as the sexual assault of children
The Trump administration has also encouraged states to pursue the death penalty and has sought more federal death sentences following Biden’s mass commutations
This year, Tennessee severely botched the attempted executions of Tony Carruthers and Christa Pike

Roughly a week after Pike survived the gruesome efforts to kill her, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the Trump administration planned to livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan , a prisoner on federal death row
But these incidents generated significant news coverage and, in Hasan’s case, mass public disapproval
Tennessee recently halted all executions, and the Trump administration backed away from livestreaming Hasan’s killing, though he will still be executed by firing squad
Reactionary efforts to shore up the death penalty might, in the end, help accelerate its decline.

title: The Download: Texas’s fragile AI boom and energy policy shifts
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout
Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts
But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position
Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat, Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor, and Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years
They won after making data centers a central issue on the campaign trail
The swings could spell trouble for hyperscalers with ambitious plans in the state
They also add to growing anxiety that America’s AI buildout could stall

Here’s how the election results could reshape AI’s future . —James O’Donnell What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections? Democrats have taken control of both the House and the Senate, but we probably won’t see major federal climate and energy legislation while Trump remains president
The midterm elections could, however, be a big deal for energy at the state and local level
The results could shape everything from the state grid and data center development to renewable energy and greenhouse gas emissions
Find out what the midterms could mean for the future of US energy . —Casey Crownhart This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter
Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday

body: A sweeping new Senate bill aims to speed up the notoriously slow US energy permitting process—but whether it helps or hurts emissions depends entirely on what gets built
The bill's backers span the political spectrum, from the White House to clean energy groups, who argue renewables stand to win economically if more building is unlocked

Critics warn the bill could open the floodgates for fossil fuel expansion, with one modeler finding it may have actually increased energy sector emissions and air pollution risks had it been in place in 2025. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148062" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US
With the dust barely settled on this week’s momentous midterms, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on November 9
It’s a plan that could finally start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved, as part of something called permitting reform
People on both sides of the political aisle have been pushing for this type of change for some years

The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still.   The federal permitting system is designed to protect the environment against industrial pollution from large projects like power plants, transmission lines, and natural-gas pipelines
Today, permitting is governed by a range of laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act
And if there’s one thing you might know about the current state of permitting in the US it’s that it’s slow and incredibly complicated
So in its 417 pages, BAAJA attempts to tighten things up

The bill has provisions that narrow the sorts of projects that need to apply for federal permits and others that enact deadlines in hopes of speeding up a process that today can take years. (There are also specific provisions about transmission planning, mining, and the rest of the kitchen sink; this thing is dense .) One thing to know about this bill is that it’s largely technology neutral: It opens the doors for the buildout of projects involving both fossil fuels and renewables
So there’s a weird mishmash of legislators and outside groups supporting it
The bill’s four sponsors in the Senate are two Republicans and two Democrats
The White House has backed this permitting reform bill, with its Council of Economic Advisors finding that it would reduce review times and have economic benefits like boosting GDP

Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s analysis finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid
Some environmental groups, however, oppose the bill, or parts of it

An assessment from the Natural Resources Defense Council says the parts about transmission could have substantial benefits for the grid, but the narrowing of environmental reviews could be damaging for public and private lands
Many in the climate world have long been calling for permitting reform, arguing that renewables stand to benefit more than fossil fuels
The thinking is that solar and wind power are some of the cheapest sources available today, so if we unlock the ability to build more energy, they are likely to win out economically
A few early analyses have tried to quantify just what BAAJA would mean for emissions in the US

One, from the think tank Rhodium Group, found that in the best-case scenario, the bill would cut economy-wide emissions by 4%, reduce annual energy bills by $78 per household, and add 200 gigawatts of new clean energy by 2040
In the worst case, emissions would stay about the same

Another report , from the nonprofit research group Resources for the Future, found that the bill could cut power-sector emissions 6% by 2041 and save more than $350 billion on system costs by midcentury
But there are some concerns that this permitting bill’s real effect would be to open the floodgates for new natural-gas plants

As data centers have put more pressure on the grid, a wave of such plants have been announced. “You get down to a trade-off between essentially growing the clean electricity industry on the one hand and then, as a compromise, growing the fossil-fuel industry on the other,” says Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue

To quantify that trade-off, Kircher also modeled the potential emissions effects of the bill and found that if BAAJA had been in place in 2025, energy sector emissions would have been higher than the actual baseline
Health and mortality risks associated with air pollution would also have increased
This bill is scheduled for a Senate vote on November 9, well before the next Congress takes control
It’s not clear what the dramatic victories for Democrats might mean for the legislation, which was expected to pass the Senate with largely Republican support if a few Democrats got on board
Democrats could decide to wait for next year, when they’ll have control of both chambers

But any deal would ultimately need to win Trump’s signature, limiting what a future bill might be able to change.  In a world where permitting new projects is easier, we’ll see more clean energy, but we’ll see more natural gas, too
And while prices could get lower, that could push demand for electricity higher, leading to more emissions overall
Simplifying the permitting system and cutting red tape is a worthy goal
But when it comes to emissions, it still really matters what, exactly, you want to build.

title: Black Michiganders helped push Abdul El-Sayed to victory – but the numbers show he was less popular with this key voting bloc than some other Democratic candidates

<title>Black Michiganders helped push Abdul El-Sayed to victory – but the numbers show he was less popular with this key voting bloc than some other Democratic candidates</title>
    <content type="html"><p>Progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/democrat-abdul-el-sayed-wins-election-to-u-s-senate-from-michigan">victory in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race</a> was one of the most-watched contests in the 2026 midterm elections. </p>

<p>As the results for this race came in, I had my eye on one demographic: Black voters. I am a <a href="https://www.bu.edu/polisci/profile/christine-slaughter/">political scientist</a> who studies Black political behavior. My research has been <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=7TP1C6cAAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;sortby=pubdate">published in numerous journals</a>, as well as in my forthcoming book, “Black Resilience,” which examines Black voters’ political participation.</p>



<h2>Wayne County voters</h2>

<p>The support of Black voters for El-Sayed was not a given. In the August primary, <a href="https://detroitmi.gov/sites/detroitmi.localhost/files/2026-08/OFFICIAL%20Election%20Summary%20Report%20-%20August%20Primary%202026.pdf">62% of Detroit voters</a> chose U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens over El-Sayed. <a href="https://www.bridgedetroit.com/detroit-is-key-to-abdul-el-sayeds-senate-bid-but-he-faces-deep-divides/">Many pundits predicted</a> it would be difficult for El-Sayed to gain support in Detroit, <a href="https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/detroitcitymichigan">which is about 75% Black</a>. </p>

<p>After the primary, El-Sayed made overtures by <a href="https://abdulforsenate.com/2026/09/thrive-transforming-housing-resources-infrastructure-value-economic-opportunities/">sharing his plans</a> to improve the lives of Black Americans, which included supporting the growth of minority-owned businesses, creating more affordable housing, eliminating food deserts and expanding the <a href="https://theconversation.com/im-a-pediatrician-in-michigan-who-created-rx-kids-one-of-the-nations-largest-anti-poverty-programs-heres-what-ive-learned-about-how-medical-schools-can-improve-community-health-277064">Rx Kids cash assistance program</a> nationwide. </p>

<p>About 91.8% of Detroit voters supported El-Sayed in the general election, <a href="https://app.enhancedvoting.com/results/public/city-detroit-mi/elections/_20261027152933">according to the city’s unofficial results</a>. Detroit City Clerk Janice Winfrey said <a href="https://www.freep.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/11/04/michigan-record-turnout-2026-midterms-blue-wave/92609483007/">209,924 residents voted in the 2026 midterms</a>, up about 21% from the 2022 midterm elections. For the 2024 presidential election, 247,770 city residents cast a ballot.</p>

<p>In fact, El-Sayed received <a href="https://apnews.com/projects/elections-2026/michigan-us-senate-results/">70.6% of Wayne County votes</a>, which includes Detroit. In 2024, Kamala Harris received <a href="https://apnews.com/projects/election-results-2024/michigan/?r=0">62.7% of the vote in Wayne County</a>. </p>

<h2>Statewide support is holding steady</h2>

<p>In the 2024 presidential election, Michigan’s <a href="https://apnews.com/projects/election-results-2024/michigan/?r=0">Democratic vote share fell to 48.3%</a>, <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Michigan_election_results,_2020">from 50.6% in 2020</a>, as the state went for Donald Trump instead of Democratic nominee Harris.  </p>

<p>Despite their ideological differences, Sen. Elissa Slotkin and El-Sayed drew <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/michigan-senate-results">similar support among Black voters.</a>  In 2024, Slotkin – a moderate Democrat – won 48.6% of the vote, a small margin over Mike Rogers, who was the Republican candidate in that race. In 2026, El-Sayed defeated Rogers statewide by a substantially wider margin, winning 52% of the vote.    </p>

<p>In other words, these early election results do not indicate whether Black voters embraced El-Sayed’s progressive platform or simply voted for the Democratic candidate. Voters may have been rejecting Republican Party politics or expressing anger toward Trump over pocketbook issues.</p>

<p>Researchers from Michigan State University found that precincts with more than 80% of Black voters <a href="https://ippsr.msu.edu/sites/default/files/mappr/ElectoralSize%26Support.pdf">supported Democratic statewide candidates</a> over Republicans at a rate of 92% to 94% during the 2024 general election, which is only slightly lower than the 94% to 95% levels observed in similar precincts during the 2020 contest between Trump and Joe Biden.</p>

<p>Even while Black voters overwhelmingly support Democrats, small shifts in their support and turnout can influence the outcome of close and competitive races. These shifts may help explain differing outcomes, including El-Sayed’s victory in 2026 and Harris’ defeat there in 2024. </p>

<p>While Black voter support for El-Sayed was high, estimated at around <a href="https://michiganchronicle.com/despite-doubts-these-detroit-voters-say-theres-excitement-for-abdul-el-sayed/">86% statewide</a>, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s support among Black voters was about 94% in the 2022 gubernatorial race, according to an <a href="https://abcnews.com/Elections/michigan-exit-polls-2022-us-governor-election-results-analysis">ABC exit poll</a>.</p>

<p>Similarly, preelection polling indicated that Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, polled <a href="https://maristpoll.marist.edu/polls/midterm-elections-in-michigan-october-2026/">more favorably among nonwhite voters compared to El-Sayed</a>. <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/michigan-senate-results">NBC exit poll data</a> shows that 86% of Black voters in Michigan supported El-Sayed, while <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/michigan-senate-results">90% supported Benson</a>, who won the governorship over Republican John James. </p>

<h2>Historic power and unity</h2>

<p>Black voters are often strategic voters who support the candidate they believe best aligns with Black interests, which has usually been the Democratic candidate since the Civil Rights Movement. </p>

<p>Generally, Black voters have made their electoral choices based on what’s believed to be best for the group as a whole – a concept described by political scientist Michael C. Dawson as <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctvzxx9d4.6">linked fate</a>. </p>

<p>However, recent research shows that Black social networks and institutions, including churches and civic organizations, reinforce expectations of <a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691199511/steadfast-democrats?srsltid=AYCX9vIo-pt1ZijIzpph8UHVplgdt7qREMzFKjFAUBo307f-9LPTnm3q">political solidarity</a>. Weaker ties to these networks may lessen the social pressure that encourages Black Americans to participate in politics and support Democratic candidates. </p>

<p>Lower participation by Black Americans could lead to elected officials paying less attention to issues important to Black voters, such as <a href="https://www.lcv.org/media-center/new-poll-ahead-of-midterms-black-and-latino-battleground-voters-rate-climate-a-high-priority-when-tied-to-affordability-and-pollution/">affordability and the cost of living, healthcare, and reducing racial discrimination</a>. If officials assume Black voters will remain loyal to Democrats, they’re under less pressure to win their votes by addressing their concerns.</p>

<p>My research has demonstrated that after the 2024 election, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11109-026-10155-6">Black women in particular felt frustrated</a> with the Democratic Party, yet they participated in elections despite these frustrations. </p>

<h2>An agenda that matters</h2>

<p>El-Sayed was part of a field of notable Democratic candidates in this election cycle. For example, Angie Nixon, a state representative in Florida, championed affordability <a href="https://19thnews.org/2026/10/angie-nixon-florida-senate-moment/">alongside a moratorium on evictions and a universal jobs program</a>, while James Talarico, a <a href="https://jamestalarico.com/issue/public-education/">former schoolteacher</a> in Texas, focused on public education.</p>

<p>El-Sayed is a former public health official who had not previously held elected office. This may have turned off some Black voters who often <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/4122905.pdf">value governing experience</a>. El-Sayed advocated for Medicare For All and lowering the costs of gas prices and groceries. </p>

<p>Although he doesn’t identify as a democratic socialist, El-Sayed campaigned with several progressive elected officials, such as U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders <a href="https://www.commondreams.org/news/abdul-el-sayed">endorsed El-Sayed</a> on the day he announced his candidacy in 2025. El-Sayed also campaigned with the Black establishment, including U.S. Rep. <a href="https://michiganadvance.com/2026/11/02/michigan-democrats-rally-behind-el-sayed-as-stevens-goes-rogue-to-support-rogers/">Jim Clyburn</a> of South Carolina. Former President <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/24/barack-obama-abdul-el-sayed-michigan">Barack Obama</a> spoke at a rally for El-Sayed in Detroit in October 2026. </p>

<p>Stevens, who <a href="https://bridgemi.com/michigan-politics/michigan-democratic-senate-primary-results-abdul-el-sayed-haley-stevens/">lost the Democratic nomination to El-Sayed</a> in the primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers after she attended a service with the Republican candidate at <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/haley-stevens-endorses-gop-mike-rogers-michigan-senate-race-el-sayed-rcna606831">a predominantly Black church in Detroit two days before the election</a>. Stevens’ tactic <a href="https://www.axios.com/2026/11/01/haley-stevens-democrats-reaction-rogers-el-sayed">drew severe backlash</a> from Democratic leaders and may have mobilized some Black voters to turn out for El-Sayed on Election Day. </p>

<p><a href="https://x.com/ABC/status/2117648241458352569">“I felt like she pimped my community,”</a> one Black voter from Detroit told ABC News in response to Stevens’ last-minute endorsement of Rogers.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289777/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770092/original/file-20261104-64-4xnjft.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C4315%2C2876&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Byron Donalds delivers his victory speech in Hollywood, Fla.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Election2026FloridaGovernor/861da958be1b46e49803e668d2864745/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=byron%20donalds%20nov%203&amp;currentItemNo=8&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In the midst of what pundits are calling a <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/04/politics/live-news/midterm-election-congress">blue tsunami nationwide</a>, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/11/03/us/elections/results-florida.html">Florida remained resolutely red</a>, electing Republican Byron Donalds as its first Black governor and sending Republican Ashley Moody back to the U.S. Senate.</p>

<p>Donalds ran on a promise to continue the <a href="https://theconversation.com/ron-desantis-2-terms-in-office-fundamentally-altered-floridas-political-landscape-cementing-conservative-policies-through-strategic-control-of-state-institutions-289946">legacy of his predecessor</a>, Gov. Ron DeSantis. </p>

<p>His victory was not as easily won as <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/florida-governor-election-polls-2026.html">polls had predicted</a>. In the week leading up to the election, polls put him at 4 points over his opponent, Democrat David Jolly. In the end, Donalds <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/11/03/us/elections/results-florida.html">won by 1.3 points</a> – about 107,000 votes.</p>

<p>I’m a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=zTrHGLoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">political scientist</a> who has lived in Florida for almost two decades and seen the powers of the governor’s office grow. We can see based on Donalds’ campaign promises the direction in which he plans to lead the state.</p>

<h2>Amendment 3 shakes things up</h2>

<p>Donalds’ term as governor will start with a major change: On Nov. 3, Floridians <a href="https://theconversation.com/florida-just-voted-for-lower-property-taxes-and-that-could-mean-cuts-in-government-services-and-new-housing-construction-295716">voted to pass Amendment 3</a> to the state constitution. </p>

<p>This will cause a shift in the state’s long-standing commitment to <a href="https://scholarship.stu.edu/faculty_articles/69/">home rule</a>, the principle that local governments, such as cities and counties, should be able to set policy on local issues.</p>

<p>The amendment <a href="https://floridapolitics.com/archives/816005-help-for-rural-coming-if-amendment-3-passes-governor-says/">limits local government spending</a> from tax revenue to core categories such as public safety, schools and natural resources. With a lower tax base, some <a href="https://floridapolitics.com/archives/816005-help-for-rural-coming-if-amendment-3-passes-governor-says/">local governments in rural areas</a> may not be able to maintain basic services and might need help from the state.</p>

<p>DeSantis has <a href="https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/state-politics/article317924418.html">called for a special session</a> to address Amendment 3 before Donalds takes office.</p>

<p>DeSantis has said he plans to restrict home rule by stopping local governments from trying to raise revenue <a href="https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/state-politics/article317924418.html">through additional taxation at the local level</a>.</p>

<p>Donalds <a href="https://www.wuft.org/politics/2026-10-01/byron-donalds-visits-uf-discusses-dei-and-amendment-3">supported the amendment</a>, and it will give him and the Legislature the opportunity to redistribute tax funding throughout the state.</p>

<p>This election has changed the makeup of the state Legislature, though, with the GOP <a href="https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/elections/2026/11/03/florida-midterm-election-results/">losing its supermajority</a> in the Florida House of Representatives, which requires holding 80 out of the 120 seats. This change in the Legislature could make it more difficult for Donalds to control the agenda in Tallahassee the way DeSantis did during his second term, when he had a supermajority in both houses of the Legislature.</p>

<p>Donalds has affirmed that he <a href="https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/elections/2026/09/29/david-jolly-byron-donalds-florida-data-centers-governor/">supports the big steps DeSantis has taken</a> to limit home rule – such as <a href="https://www.tallahassee.com/story/news/state/2026/04/14/planning-law-limiting-local-governments-in-florida/89553404007/">limiting local control over land development</a> and <a href="https://floridaphoenix.com/2023/08/09/desantis-ousts-another-democratic-prosecutor-monique-worrell-of-orange-county/">removing local elected officials</a> from office – and plans to <a href="https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/elections/2026/09/29/david-jolly-byron-donalds-florida-data-centers-governor/">take executive authority further</a>, scheduling more DOGE audits of local government and removing more elected officials as he sees fit.</p>

<p>When it comes to data centers, on the other hand, Donalds has said he favors <a href="https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/elections/2026/09/29/david-jolly-byron-donalds-florida-data-centers-governor/">local communities deciding</a> whether to allow them to be built nearby.</p>
