<h2>Florida health policy on vaccine mandates</h2>

<p>One of the first choices awaiting Donalds will be whom to appoint as Florida surgeon general, a position <a href="https://www.floridahealth.gov/about-us/">created in 2007</a>. The position comes with the power to <a href="https://floridapolitics.com/archives/473446-lawmakers-ok-bills-to-limit-surgeon-general-emergency-powers/">declare public health emergencies</a>, forcibly quarantine people and <a href="https://floridatrident.org/repeal-of-vaccine-mandates-faces-legal-challenges/">set vaccine mandates for illnesses such as chickenpox</a> that fall outside the state Legislature’s framework of <a href="https://floridatrident.org/repeal-of-vaccine-mandates-faces-legal-challenges/">seven childhood vaccine mandates</a>.</p>

<p>As part of his <a href="https://theconversation.com/ron-desantis-2-terms-in-office-fundamentally-altered-floridas-political-landscape-cementing-conservative-policies-through-strategic-control-of-state-institutions-289946">conservative remake of Florida policies</a>, DeSantis appointed the current surgeon general, <a href="https://www.floridahealth.gov/about-us/leadership/state-surgeon-general/">Dr. Joseph Ladapo</a>, to the position in 2021. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Ladapo emerged as a leading <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/consumer-health/health-freedom-movement/">medical freedom</a> advocate and vaccine skeptic.</p>

<p>Ladapo <a href="https://abcnews.com/Health/florida-surgeon-general-state-moving-end-vaccine-mandates/story?id=125224527">opposes all vaccine mandates</a>. He also proposed new Florida health rules in October 2026 to <a href="https://floridaphoenix.com/2026/10/08/ladapo-eliminating-vaccine-mandates-isnt-about-science-its-about-parents-rights/">drop mandates for four vaccines</a> required for school attendance, including chickenpox and hepatitis B. Currently, <a href="https://www.floridahealth.gov/individual-family-health/immunization/parents-children-and-adolescents/exemption-from-required-immunizations/">the state allows exemptions</a> only for approved religious or medical reasons.</p>

<p>The Florida Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics <a href="https://www.fcaap.org/posts/news/florida-pediatricians-testify-against-proposed-rule-weakening-school-immunization-requirements/">opposes the rule change</a> on public health grounds.</p>

<p>Donalds has long <a href="https://donalds.house.gov/news/email/show.aspx?ID=B5G6AKCJWTTEQ">opposed vaccine mandates</a> and says that he <a href="https://edition.cnn.com/videos/politics/2021/07/27/byron-donalds-florida-coronavirus-vaccine-cuomo-intv-vpx.cnn">did not personally receive a COVID-19 vaccine</a>. He <a href="https://www.wusf.org/politics-issues/2026-09-23/donalds-might-retain-joseph-ladapo-as-surgeon-general-jolly-says-hed-fire-him">supports Ladapo’s proposed rule change</a> to reduce school vaccination mandates and said during his campaign that he is <a href="https://www.wusf.org/politics-issues/2026-09-23/donalds-might-retain-joseph-ladapo-as-surgeon-general-jolly-says-hed-fire-him">open to reappointing Ladapo</a> as surgeon general.</p>

<p>The Florida Legislature, however, will limit how far Donalds can push vaccine policy. The <a href="https://mynews13.com/fl/orlando/news/2026/08/14/new-federal-vaccine-guidance-raises-questions-for-florida-families-but-school-requirements-remain-unchanged">Legislature has mandated</a> measles and polio vaccines for all K-12 public school students, so getting rid of that requirement would require a change in the law.</p>

<h2>Universal school vouchers</h2>

<p>One of the biggest developments in Florida K-12 education in recent years has been the creation of a system of <a href="https://theconversation.com/floridas-school-choice-program-offers-universal-vouchers-but-cannot-show-systemwide-academic-improvement-283040">universal vouchers</a> by DeSantis and the Legislature in 2023. This program allows <a href="https://www.stepupforstudents.org/scholarships/">parents of any income level</a> to use <a href="https://go.stepupforstudents.org/hubfs/Scholarship%20Info/FTC-FES-EO-PEP-Award-Amounts.pdf">US$8,000 in state money on average, based on county of residence</a>, for their children’s private or homeschooling education.</p>

<p>The universal voucher program has created intense pressure on the state budget. It cost an <a href="https://www.tampabay.com/news/education/2026/05/27/vouchers-grow-floridas-budget-will-there-be-added-accountability/">estimated $4.5 billion in fiscal year 2026</a>. State auditors have identified <a href="https://mynews13.com/fl/orlando/news/2025/12/04/audit-finds-fl-vouchers-program-has-trouble-tracking-millions">accountability problems</a> in tracking funds through the system. Public schools have faced <a href="https://hechingerreport.org/universal-vouchers-have-public-schools-worried-about-something-new-market-share/">declining enrollment</a>, with fewer resources to serve the neediest students they cannot turn away.</p>

<p>Donalds strongly supports the universal voucher program. He has expressed an interest in making Florida “<a href="https://floridatrib.org/2026/07/30/what-byron-and-erika-donalds-gospel-of-school-choice-could-mean-for-florida/">the model state for school choice</a>” by <a href="https://www.miaminewtimes.com/news/the-billionaire-trying-to-reinvent-florida-schools-has-a-7-5-million-bet-on-byron-donalds-40565603/">allowing parents to choose among private educational providers competing in the marketplace</a>.</p>

<p>His wife, Erika Donalds, is a former Collier County school board member who operates a <a href="https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/election/article317723535.html">network of for-profit charter schools</a> and <a href="https://floridatrib.org/2026/07/30/what-byron-and-erika-donalds-gospel-of-school-choice-could-mean-for-florida/">advocates nationally for school choice</a>. Whether the Donaldses will <a href="https://www.wlrn.org/government-politics/2026-11-03/byron-donalds-makes-history-as-states-first-black-governor">divest from the charter school business</a> during the governor-elect’s term remains to be seen.</p>

<p>Already, the governor-elect has <a href="https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-government/state-politics/article317924418.html">indicated</a> that he might work with the Legislature to change the way the Florida Education Finance Program funds K-12 schools, allowing districts to spend funds with more flexibility.</p>

<p>During his campaign he also proposed a <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/teacher-pay-vouchers-candidates-florida-195700038.html">universal scorecard</a> for the voucher program so that parents can compare educational data on student performance across different types of schools. Currently, only public schools must provide this data.</p>

<p>Donalds can also influence state education policy by <a href="https://www.fldoe.org/policy/state-board-of-edu/">appointing the seven members of the Board of Education</a> and then recommending a candidate for <a href="https://www.fldoe.org/about-us/commissioner/">commissioner of education</a> for that board to elect. The commissioner and state board oversee the <a href="https://www.fldoe.org/">Florida Department of Education</a> and programs from kindergarten through postsecondary education.</p>

<p>They board could also implement new eligibility rules for private school vouchers, <a href="https://www.flgov.com/eog/news/press/2023/florida-takes-action-against-four-florida-schools-ties-chinese-communist-party">as the DeSantis administration</a> <a href="https://www.tallahassee.com/story/news/state/2026/10/15/florida-school-vouchers-could-be-banned-for-some-islamic-schools/91705943007/">has done</a> in the past.</p>

<h2>The way forward</h2>

<p>During his campaign, Donalds attempted to <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/m-allowed-own-viewpoint-byron-090000377.html">distance himself from President Donald Trump</a>, whose policies have proven unpopular even in red states such as Florida. </p>

<p>But in his <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qc9qAcp-PCE">victory speech on the evening of Nov. 3</a>, Donalds proudly announced that he had received a congratulatory call from the president. “Mr. President,” he said to a cheering crowd, “I want you to hear from Florida that we are still red.”</p>

<p><em>This story is an update of a <a href="https://theconversation.com/3-major-issues-that-republican-byron-donalds-or-democrat-david-jolly-will-need-to-address-as-floridas-next-governor-293784">story published on Oct. 28, 2026</a>.</em>

<title>Delayed international support has hampered efforts to contain and treat Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769839/original/file-20261103-64-hjk74y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5760%2C3840&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The DRC is in the seventh month of an Ebola outbreak.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/CongoEbola/3e6ea3d3e00042c7a8dde24ec4ac40f8/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=ebola%202026&amp;currentItemNo=2&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Sebastien Kitsa Musayi</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>I visited a family of 19 in Sierra Leone in 2015. By the time I arrived, eight had died. The other 11 were left to live with the grief and fear of what might happen next. </p>

<p>I am a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ql73QjkAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">medical doctor and epidemiologist</a>, and at that time I was serving on an African Union Ebola response mission. The <a href="https://www.who.int/emergencies/situations/ebola-outbreak-2014-2016-West-Africa">2014-16 epidemic in West Africa</a> caused more than 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths. Over roughly six months in Sierra Leone, I saw how quickly the disease could overwhelm families and health services.</p>

<p>That’s also when I learned that good medical advice can fail if people do not trust those delivering it. Some families buried relatives secretly, despite warnings. In certain communities, funeral practices included <a href="https://www.theopennotebook.com/2017/10/03/storygram-amy-maxmens-how-the-fight-against-ebola-tested-a-cultures-traditions/">washing the body and sprinkling water on mourners</a>, which risked exposing people to infected bodily fluids.</p>

<p>Simply repeating instructions did not help. But those of us working in the field found that working with families to make burials safer while respecting their grief helped them to mourn their loss while stopping the virus from spreading.</p>

<p>More than a decade later, those experiences have returned to my mind. The Ebola outbreak <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/ebola/situation-summary/index.html">now sweeping across parts of Central Africa</a> is different from the one I responded to. Still, one lesson remains: Timely international support makes a huge difference.</p>

<h2>A growing outbreak</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/05/17/africa/ebola-outbreak-congo-uganda-explainer-intl">current outbreak was declared</a> in the Democratic Republic of Congo, or DRC, in May 2026. By Oct. 28, 2026, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/ebola/situation-summary/index.html">reported 10,305 confirmed cases</a> and 4,996 deaths across five countries, with new updates daily. The DRC accounts for nearly all of those cases and deaths.</p>

<p>This is already the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/30/world/africa/ebola-deaths-record.html">second-largest Ebola outbreak</a> ever recorded, after the 2014-16 epidemic. </p>

<p>The current outbreak is caused by the <a href="https://theconversation.com/ebola-strain-spreading-in-congo-and-uganda-has-no-approved-vaccine-283221">Bundibugyo virus</a>, whereas the 2014-16 epidemic involved a different Ebola virus. No vaccine or specific treatment is currently approved for Bundibugyo.</p>

<p>The World Health Organization warns that late detection, deaths outside health facilities and sustained transmission in the DRC <a href="https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2026-DON622">remain serious concerns</a>.</p>

<p>The DRC has <a href="https://cbs.ifrc.org/implementations/democratic-republic-congo">extensive experience with responding to outbreaks</a>, and African institutions are <a href="https://www.afro.who.int/countries/uganda/news/who-africa-cdc-launch-continental-incident-management-support-team-strengthen-coordination-ebola">coordinating a continental response</a>. Africa has the expertise and leadership. What it needs right now is sustained support that reaches the front line – quickly, safely and accountably.</p>

<h2>Crossing borders</h2>

<p>Ebola follows human movement. In October, <a href="https://abcnews.com/International/kenya-confirms-8th-case-ebola-infections-linked-back/story?id=137374403">Kenya reported infections linked to a traveler</a> who had passed through Uganda from the DRC. Nigeria also <a href="https://afro.who.int/countries/nigeria/news/nigeria-confirms-imported-case-ebola-bundibugyo-virus-disease">reported an imported case</a> around the same time.</p>

<p>Symptoms can appear between two and 21 days after exposure, and people are generally not infectious before symptoms begin. A traveler may therefore pass a temperature check and become ill days later.</p>

<p>These events show why countries need to share information quickly, verify travel histories and maintain contact tracing across borders. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769843/original/file-20261103-64-scvmcq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="a row of canvas tents with people walking around outside" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769843/original/file-20261103-64-scvmcq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769843/original/file-20261103-64-scvmcq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769843/original/file-20261103-64-scvmcq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769843/original/file-20261103-64-scvmcq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769843/original/file-20261103-64-scvmcq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769843/original/file-20261103-64-scvmcq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769843/original/file-20261103-64-scvmcq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">In response to the 2014 Ebola outbreak, American healthcare workers set up makeshift clinics like this one outside Monrovia, Liberia.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/EbolaAid/3c5aebb5d5964e869fb356e821dcb0d8/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=ebola%20international%20aid%202014&amp;currentItemNo=4&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">Abbas Dulleh/AP</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What international support looks like now</h2>

<p>International partners are, in fact, contributing. In September 2026, the United States reported <a href="https://www.globalsecurity.org/security/library/news/2026/09/sec-260923-state01.htm">US$887 million in Ebola-related health and humanitarian assistance</a>. The U.K. announced a <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-accelerates-support-for-efforts-to-stop-ebola-outbreak-at-source">contribution of roughly £78 million ($104 million)</a>.</p>

<p>In October, the World Bank described <a href="https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2026/10/13/world-bank-group-expands-ongoing-support-for-ebola-response-in-drc-and-the-region">$426.6 million in current and planned financing</a> for the DRC and neighboring countries. And Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly <a href="https://africacdc.org/news-item/g20-mobilises-us2-9-billion-for-ebola-response-as-africa-cdc-calls-for-full-transparency-and-traceability-of-every-dollar/">$3 billion in international pledges</a> following a September mobilization effort.</p>

<p>But pledges are not the same as supplies delivered or services provided, and these contributions are coming late in the outbreak.</p>

<p>In 2014, Britain helped <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/heapol/czy102">expand treatment and safe-burial operations</a> in Sierra Leone. The U.S. mobilized logistics capacity in Liberia, while France assisted Guinea. And African Union health workers served alongside local teams and other partners.</p>

<p>That cooperation saved lives, though the global response was slow to scale up. It has been discouraging for me to see that today’s response has not built on that experience without waiting for the outbreak to grow further.</p>

<p>According to the WHO, <a href="https://www.who.int/news/item/28-08-2026-second-meeting-of-the-ihr-emergency-committee-on-the-epidemic-of-ebola-bundibugyo-virus-disease-in-the-democratic-republic-of-the-congo---meeting-report?utm">massive cuts to international aid</a> over the past year diminished a quicker response.</p>

<p>The success of international collaboration will be measured in how many contacts are reached, how rapidly patients are tested, how many health workers have protective equipment and are consistently paid, whether women can still deliver babies safely, and whether remote communities can get care.</p>

<h2>Building connections with everyday people</h2>

<p>My experience in Sierra Leone in 2014 taught me that trust is essential to outbreak control. Families need credible explanations, timely information and opportunities to ask questions. Local health workers, faith leaders, survivors and community organizations can help bridge the gap between an emergency response and the people it seeks to protect.</p>

<p>That gap can be large even when a disease is widely known. A colleague and I conducted a study involving 440 secondary school students in Nigeria in 2014, and we found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/currents.outbreaks.c04b88cd5cd03cccb99e125657eecd76">95.4% had heard of Ebola</a>. Yet only 42.3% identified fever as a possible symptom, and only 33.2% recognized the risk associated with certain burial practices. Seeing that awareness of the disease alone was not enough, we subsequently began Ebola education activities in local Nigerian schools.</p>

<p>The need for reliable information from trusted sources remains in 2026. Risk messages must be consistent, culturally sensitive and practical. This works only when communities are partners in recognizing illness, seeking early care, contact follow-up and safe, dignified burials. Even in times of emergency, health workers cannot treat communities simply as audiences for instructions.</p>

<h2>Reaching affected communities</h2>

<p>In August 2026, Africa CDC and the WHO jointly called for <a href="https://www.who.int/news/item/06-08-2026-africa-cdc-and-who-call-for-urgent--community-led-action-to-contain-ebola-in-the-drc">expanded laboratory and treatment capacity</a> and faster delivery of supplies.</p>

<p>But in the DRC, insecurity and displacement <a href="https://www.cfr.org/global-conflict-tracker/conflict/violence-democratic-republic-congo">due to ongoing conflict</a>, in addition to poor roads, can prevent supplies and patients from reaching treatment centers. These obstacles may also keep laboratories from receiving samples and contact-tracing teams from visiting households.</p>

<p>The ministry of health is not equipped to resolve these problems. The response therefore requires cooperation among health authorities, humanitarian agencies, local government, transport services and those responsible for civilian safety.</p>

<p>There are signs that investments in these services are helping. In October, the World Bank reported that <a href="https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2026/10/13/world-bank-group-expands-ongoing-support-for-ebola-response-in-drc-and-the-region">supported detection timelines in the DRC had improved</a>. This meant new cases were being detected within one or two days by September, a huge improvement from the 10-day detection timeline early in the outbreak.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769838/original/file-20261103-64-28fiz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="woman in hair net and gloves gives shot to a man in short sleeves" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769838/original/file-20261103-64-28fiz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769838/original/file-20261103-64-28fiz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769838/original/file-20261103-64-28fiz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769838/original/file-20261103-64-28fiz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769838/original/file-20261103-64-28fiz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769838/original/file-20261103-64-28fiz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769838/original/file-20261103-64-28fiz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The Tumaini vaccine trials started in the DRC at the end of October 2026. ‘Tumaini’ is the Swahili word for hope.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/CongoEbola/e75b48e4b940466e82f3d4137a518120/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=ebola%202026&amp;currentItemNo=20&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Dieudonne Dirole</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Looking to the future</h2>

<p>Because Bundibugyo virus lacks an approved vaccine or specific treatment, this outbreak also demands carefully conducted research. The <a href="https://www.itg.be/en/health-stories/press-releases/tumaini-first-participant-vaccinated">Tumaini vaccine trial</a>, begun in Bunia, DRC, in October 2026, is an important step toward a potential vaccine.</p>

<p>The hope is that this effort will prevent more families from experiencing loss.</p>

<p>I still remember the 11 survivors in that Sierra Leone household I visited back in 2015. I never learned what ultimately happened to them, but more than a decade later, I still think about them.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295610/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Mammograms can do more than detect breast cancer – they also offer important clues on heart health</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770127/original/file-20261104-64-ul5ctf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5760%2C3840&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Breast arterial calcification, or BAC, is easily visible on mammograms, and research shows it can add important insights about a woman&#39;s risk of heart disease or stroke.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/medical-technician-taking-mammogram-exam-to-female-royalty-free-image/1457021971">peakSTOCK/iStock via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>If you’re a woman over 40, you have no doubt heard your doctor tell you to get a mammogram as part of <a href="https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/breast-cancer-screening">routine screening for breast cancer</a>. But there’s another reason, too.  </p>

<p>A mammogram can show no sign of breast cancer and still reveal something worth discussing with a doctor: calcium deposits in the medium-sized arteries that carry blood to the breast. These calcium deposits may offer a clue to a woman’s future heart health.</p>

<p>I’m a <a href="https://pure.psu.edu/en/persons/matthew-nudy/">cardiologist</a> who studies <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecl.2026.08.001">cardiovascular health around menopause</a>. My colleagues and I have investigated how mammograms might help identify women who are at <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amjcard.2026.01.014">increased risk of heart disease and stroke</a>. Artificial intelligence now makes these calcium deposits – called <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s44325-026-00135-4">breast arterial calcification</a>, or BAC – easier to measure. </p>

<p>In October 2026, Maryland became the first U.S. state to <a href="https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Legislation/Details/hb1364?ys=2026RS">require mammography centers to notify patients in writing</a> if these calcium deposits are found in their mammograms. Other states may institute similar rules soon. Research shows that these calcium deposits are a robust marker for cardiovascular risk, and I expect its adoption to grow.</p>

<p>Here’s what women need to know about calcium deposits in the breast – and what they should do if their mammogram shows they have them. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/A-yGCQdZ68o?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Mammography centers in Maryland must now inform patients if their breast scans show breast arterial calcification.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What is breast arterial calcification?</h2>

<p>Breast arterial calcification is calcium buildup in the walls of medium-sized arteries that carry blood through the breast. On a mammogram image, the calcium deposits appear as parallel white lines tracing those vessels.</p>

<p>This finding is not a sign of breast cancer. And it differs from the fatty and calcified <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/16753-atherosclerosis-arterial-disease">plaque that can narrow arteries</a> supplying the heart muscle. In the case of breast arterial calcification, the calcium lies mainly in the artery’s muscular wall, where it is associated with blood vessel stiffening. </p>

<p>Finding breast arterial calcification on a mammogram does not, by itself, establish that a woman has heart disease or a blocked heart artery. But research has now clearly shown that this marker signals that a person’s risk of these outcomes is elevated.</p>

<p>It’s important to remember, however, that its absence does not rule out cardiovascular disease or an increased risk of heart attack or stroke. </p>



<h2>A well-studied connection</h2>

<p>Doctors have known about breast arterial calcification for decades, with studies in the 1980s linking it to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1148/radiology.136.1.7384525">diabetes</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.2214/ajr.148.5.855">advanced kidney disease</a>. Early findings about its <a href="https://doi.org/10.1148/radiol.09090102">relationship with heart disease were mixed</a>, and many studies were small and relied on radiologists’ visual review of mammograms. </p>

<p>In 2022, my colleagues and I published the results of a 10-year study in which radiologists reviewed mammograms of more than 1,000 women to identify these calcium deposits. Women who had them had about <a href="https://doi.org/10.1097/gme.0000000000002088">three times the odds of developing coronary heart disease</a> and five times the odds of having a stroke compared with women who didn’t, even after taking age into account.</p>

<p>To confirm that breast arterial calcification in mammograms predicts cardiovascular risk, we assessed <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amjcard.2026.01.014">45 published studies involving more than 68,000 women</a>, in a type of study called a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1752-8062.2009.00152.x">meta-analysis</a>. This work, published in 2026, found that women who had these calcium deposits in their breast arteries on a mammogram had roughly twice the risk of stroke, heart failure and death from any cause, and nearly three times the risk of dying from heart disease, compared with women who did not. </p>

<p>The studies we analyzed differed considerably in design and quality, so these averages cannot precisely predict an individual woman’s cardiovascular risk. Also, while these findings establish an association between breast arterial calcification and cardiovascular disease, they do not show that calcium in the breast arteries causes those health outcomes.</p>

<h2>Integrating AI and age</h2>

<p>Radiologists can see breast artery calcium on a routine mammogram. But there’s no common standard for grading and reporting how much calcification is present. AI tools which are being used more commonly by doctors can measure how much is there using the same images, with no extra radiation.</p>

<p>These calcium deposits become more common with age, so my colleagues and I used AI to assess data from more than <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcmg.2026.03.008">100,000 women in nine countries</a> in order to map how calcium builds up in breast arteries by age. We developed and tested a metric that, when added to standard tools, improved doctors’ ability to accurately predict a woman’s risk of cardiovascular disease. </p>

<h2>Integrating as a new risk marker</h2>

<p>Maryland became the first state to require a notice about breast arterial calcification in screening results. The goal is to give women who have it a reason to talk with their doctor about heart health. </p>

<p>The bill’s sponsor modeled the law on a <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-fdas-rule-change-requiring-providers-to-inform-women-about-breast-density-could-lead-to-a-flurry-of-questions-201951">2023 regulation on breast density notices</a>, which required mammography centers to inform patients and their doctors about their breast density and its link to cancer detection. The breast density rule was <a href="https://www.auntminnie.com/clinical-news/womens-imaging/breast/article/15614230/10-states-introduced-breast-density-laws-this-year">first implemented in Connecticut</a> and then adopted by many other states, before <a href="https://www.fda.gov/radiation-emitting-products/mammography-quality-standards-act-mqsa-and-mqsa-program/important-information-final-rule-amend-mammography-quality-standards-act-mqsa">becoming a nationwide requirement</a>. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770163/original/file-20261104-64-u3ef3y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A doctor takes a female patient's blood pressure." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770163/original/file-20261104-64-u3ef3y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770163/original/file-20261104-64-u3ef3y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770163/original/file-20261104-64-u3ef3y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770163/original/file-20261104-64-u3ef3y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770163/original/file-20261104-64-u3ef3y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770163/original/file-20261104-64-u3ef3y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770163/original/file-20261104-64-u3ef3y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Calcium deposits on a mammogram don’t cause heart disease, and their discovery does not mean you have it. But they may increase your risk.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/taking-patients-blood-pressure-royalty-free-image/532743068">Dann Tardif/Stone via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>An Australian <a href="https://www.anzctr.org.au/Trial/Registration/TrialReview.aspx?ACTRN=12626000822381">trial called TIM-TAM</a> will test whether using breast arterial calcification to guide care improves measures of heart health. Researchers still need to find out whether treating women based on the presence of breast arterial calcification prevents heart attacks or strokes. But research already shows that the marker has a link to cardiovascular disease, and I expect it to follow a similar pattern of adoption as reporting breast density.</p>

<p>Until other states adjust their requirements, look for “breast arterial calcification” or “vascular calcifications” in the radiologist’s report. Mammography centers’ reporting practices vary, so some reports may omit BAC even when it’s visible. Some imaging centers offer an optional AI review for breast arterial calcification as an out-of-pocket add-on to a screening mammogram. </p>

<h2>What this means for your care</h2>

<p>On its own, the presence of breast arterial calcification on a mammogram does not determine whether someone needs a heart test or a new prescription. But in my view, this marker can provide a useful nudge to get an updated assessment of cardiovascular health.</p>

<p>Your doctor may suggest a blood pressure measurement and blood tests for cholesterol and kidney function. <a href="https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/estimated-glomerular-filtration-rate-egfr">An estimate called eGFR</a> describes how well the kidneys filter blood. </p>

<p>Your doctor can use these results alongside age, smoking, diabetes and other information in the <a href="https://professional.heart.org/en/guidelines-and-statements/prevent-calculator">American Heart Association’s PREVENT calculator</a>. It estimates the chance of developing cardiovascular disease over the next 10 years for adults ages 30 to 79 who are not already diagnosed with cardiovascular disease.</p>

<p>You can then discuss with your doctor which steps could make the biggest difference for your heart health depending on your risk. That might mean finding ways to move more, choosing foods that are good for your heart or getting help to quit smoking if you smoke. Depending on your overall risk, your doctor may also suggest taking a statin to lower your cholesterol or starting or adjusting blood pressure medicine. These treatments can help lower your chances of a heart attack or stroke.</p>

<p>A routine breast screening visit can thus become an opportunity to help women understand their cardiovascular risk and take steps to lower it.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294073/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Breast arterial calcification, or BAC, is easily visible on mammograms, and research shows it can add important insights about a woman's risk of heart disease or stroke. peakSTOCK/iStock via Getty Images If you’re a woman over 40, you have no doubt heard your doctor tell you to get a mammogram as part of routine screening for breast cancer
A mammogram can show no sign of breast cancer and still reveal something worth discussing with a doctor: calcium deposits in the medium-sized arteries that carry blood to the breast
These calcium deposits may offer a clue to a woman’s future heart health
I’m a cardiologist who studies cardiovascular health around menopause
My colleagues and I have investigated how mammograms might help identify women who are at increased risk of heart disease and stroke
Artificial intelligence now makes these calcium deposits – called breast arterial calcification , or BAC – easier to measure
In October 2026, Maryland became the first U.S. state to require mammography centers to notify patients in writing if these calcium deposits are found in their mammograms
Other states may institute similar rules soon
Research shows that these calcium deposits are a robust marker for cardiovascular risk, and I expect its adoption to grow
Here’s what women need to know about calcium deposits in the breast – and what they should do if their mammogram shows they have them
Mammography centers in Maryland must now inform patients if their breast scans show breast arterial calcification
What is breast arterial calcification? Breast arterial calcification is calcium buildup in the walls of medium-sized arteries that carry blood through the breast
On a mammogram image, the calcium deposits appear as parallel white lines tracing those vessels
This finding is not a sign of breast cancer
And it differs from the fatty and calcified plaque that can narrow arteries supplying the heart muscle
In the case of breast arterial calcification, the calcium lies mainly in the artery’s muscular wall, where it is associated with blood vessel stiffening
Finding breast arterial calcification on a mammogram does not, by itself, establish that a woman has heart disease or a blocked heart artery
But research has now clearly shown that this marker signals that a person’s risk of these outcomes is elevated
It’s important to remember, however, that its absence does not rule out cardiovascular disease or an increased risk of heart attack or stroke
A well-studied connection Doctors have known about breast arterial calcification for decades, with studies in the 1980s linking it to diabetes and advanced kidney disease
Early findings about its relationship with heart disease were mixed , and many studies were small and relied on radiologists’ visual review of mammograms
In 2022, my colleagues and I published the results of a 10-year study in which radiologists reviewed mammograms of more than 1,000 women to identify these calcium deposits
Women who had them had about three times the odds of developing coronary heart disease and five times the odds of having a stroke compared with women who didn’t, even after taking age into account
To confirm that breast arterial calcification in mammograms predicts cardiovascular risk, we assessed 45 published studies involving more than 68,000 women , in a type of study called a meta-analysis

This work, published in 2026, found that women who had these calcium deposits in their breast arteries on a mammogram had roughly twice the risk of stroke, heart failure and death from any cause, and nearly three times the risk of dying from heart disease, compared with women who did not
The studies we analyzed differed considerably in design and quality, so these averages cannot precisely predict an individual woman’s cardiovascular risk
Also, while these findings establish an association between breast arterial calcification and cardiovascular disease, they do not show that calcium in the breast arteries causes those health outcomes
Integrating AI and age Radiologists can see breast artery calcium on a routine mammogram
But there’s no common standard for grading and reporting how much calcification is present
AI tools which are being used more commonly by doctors can measure how much is there using the same images, with no extra radiation

These calcium deposits become more common with age, so my colleagues and I used AI to assess data from more than 100,000 women in nine countries in order to map how calcium builds up in breast arteries by age
We developed and tested a metric that, when added to standard tools, improved doctors’ ability to accurately predict a woman’s risk of cardiovascular disease
Integrating as a new risk marker Maryland became the first state to require a notice about breast arterial calcification in screening results
The goal is to give women who have it a reason to talk with their doctor about heart health

The bill’s sponsor modeled the law on a 2023 regulation on breast density notices , which required mammography centers to inform patients and their doctors about their breast density and its link to cancer detection
The breast density rule was first implemented in Connecticut and then adopted by many other states, before becoming a nationwide requirement
Calcium deposits on a mammogram don’t cause heart disease, and their discovery does not mean you have it
Dann Tardif/Stone via Getty Images An Australian trial called TIM-TAM will test whether using breast arterial calcification to guide care improves measures of heart health
Researchers still need to find out whether treating women based on the presence of breast arterial calcification prevents heart attacks or strokes
But research already shows that the marker has a link to cardiovascular disease, and I expect it to follow a similar pattern of adoption as reporting breast density

<title>I research play – and here’s why recess is much more important than just a fun break</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770108/original/file-20261104-64-d5jahe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C66%2C5378%2C3585&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The amount of time children spend at recess varies considerably. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/children-running-on-playground-royalty-free-image/515286545?phrase=Recess%20kids&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Dan Kenyon/Stock Photos via Getty Images </a></span></figcaption></figure><p>School recess has long been considered a standard part of children’s education in the United States. But it’s more than just a fun break from sitting at a desk. </p>

<p>Daily recess is necessary for supporting young children and adolescents’ learning, as well as their <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph22101469">physical and mental health</a>. </p>

<p>It’s so important that the American Academy of Pediatrics <a href="https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2026-077025">notes that reducing the amount of time</a> set aside for playing, running and exploring in order to fit in more academic work could actually be counterproductive. </p>

<p>But in recent decades many schools have cut back on recess, which many states <a href="https://americanhealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2026-01/Recess%20Policy%20Package%202025_1.pdf">do not require</a>. </p>

<p>As <a href="https://www.gse.harvard.edu/directory/faculty/louisa-penfold">a scholar</a> who researches childhood play, I have studied and witnessed the benefits of play in children’s lives, including the significant social, emotional and cognitive impacts it has on students’ overall well-being.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770115/original/file-20261104-64-o6t619.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A group of children play and hang from monkey bars in a yard." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770115/original/file-20261104-64-o6t619.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770115/original/file-20261104-64-o6t619.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=476&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770115/original/file-20261104-64-o6t619.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=476&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770115/original/file-20261104-64-o6t619.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=476&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770115/original/file-20261104-64-o6t619.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=598&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770115/original/file-20261104-64-o6t619.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=598&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770115/original/file-20261104-64-o6t619.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=598&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Most states do not require that schools have recess every day.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/children-in-playground-royalty-free-image/84663562?phrase=kids%20playing%20recess&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">John P Kelly/Stone via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The many benefits of recess</h2>

<p>The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that children and adolescents get at least <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/physical-activity-education/about/index.html">60 minutes of physical activity</a> per day. </p>

<p>The CDC also <a href="https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/healthyschools/physicalactivity/pdf/Recess_All_Students.pdf">defines recess</a> as a “regularly scheduled period in the school day for physical activity and play that is monitored by trained staff or volunteers.”</p>

<p>Recess can look different across various schools – while some kids play outside on play structures or in grassy fields, others might play indoors during inclement weather. </p>

<p>Research also shows, for example, that children living in lower-income communities have <a href="https://kaboom.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Review-Playspace-Equity-Children.pdf">fewer opportunities</a> than their peers in higher-income communities to play outside. </p>

<p>Unlike physical education classes or participating in organized sports, recess gives students the time to engage in physical activity and interact with their peers however they like.</p>

<p>This time for unstructured play can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.13230">offer much-needed relief</a> from the mental focus that students need to maintain throughout the school day. It can also support <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/1132190">their cognitive development</a> and overall emotional and physical well-being. </p>

<p>Research also consistently shows that giving children breaks each day for recess has immense benefits for their mental health and the <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17165972">executive functioning skills</a> that support academic achievement. </p>

<p>This includes benefits for students’ <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10984-017-9237-x">focus and creativity</a>, as well as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1123/pes.2013-0141">their memory</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17165972">executive function</a>. </p>

<h2>Some states, but not all, require recess</h2>

<p><a href="https://americanhealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2026-01/Recess%20Policy%20Package%202025_1.pdf">Most states do not mandate</a> that schools have recess every day or  spell out a minimum amount of time students must spend moving their bodies. </p>

<p>A <a href="https://americanhealth.jhu.edu/recess-in-schools">2025 report</a> from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health found that 11 states have laws addressing school recess. This ranges from Arizona’s requirement for 40 minutes of daily recess to Georgia, Indiana and Kentucky all requiring recess, but with no minimum duration. </p>

<p>Massachusetts is one of the nearly 40 states without any laws regarding recess time. A <a href="https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/09/17/metro/recess/">recent article</a> in The Boston Globe reported schools in Cambridge having 25 minutes of recess, while other schools across the state had only 15 minutes per day. </p>

<p>Overall, there has been an <a href="https://tnhousegop.org/press-releases/2025/04/rep-scott-cepicky-passes-bill-increasing-access-to-recess-for-tennessee-students/">uptick in state legislation</a> aimed at preserving mandated daily school recess time, thanks partly to a new parent-led advocacy group called <a href="https://www.sayyestorecess.com/home">Say Yes to Recess</a>. This group is pushing for schools across the country to provide a minimum of 60 minutes of protected school recess time each day. </p>

<p>Started by three Tennessee moms, Say Yes to Recess has also helped advocate for Tennessee legislation that increased the state’s mandated daily school recess time <a href="https://tnhousegop.org/press-releases/2025/04/rep-scott-cepicky-passes-bill-increasing-access-to-recess-for-tennessee-students/">from 15 to 40 minutes</a> in July 2025. </p>

<h2>A moving target</h2>

<p>During the 2001-02 school year, elementary school students from 349 school districts spent on average <a href="https://doi.org/10.3200/AEPR.109.6.23-28">36.8 minutes</a> per day at recess. </p>

<p>By 2025, the <a href="https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/healthyschools/physicalactivity/pdf/Recess_All_Students.pdf">CDC found</a> that students were spending 27 minutes on average in recess each day. </p>

<p>It’s also hard to track how much physical activity students get at school because public school districts and private schools often do not record and report this information.</p>

<p>While the benefits of recess are not just <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.psicoe.2024.02.003">isolated to young children</a>, a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/21594937.2025.2611562">2026 international study</a> showed that the amount of daily recess time across U.S. schools declines from a mean of 39.3 minutes per day for 6- to 7-year-olds to 24.5 minutes per day for 12- to 18-year-olds. </p>

<h2>Making way for play</h2>

<p>I conducted research at the <a href="https://pz.harvard.edu/">Project Zero research center</a> for creativity, ethics and the arts at Harvard University and highlighted the significance of play and the arts within urban public schools. </p>

<p>This <a href="https://pz.harvard.edu/resources/artplay-final-report">2024 study</a> showed how play with materials supports both children’s and teachers’ creative learning. As someone who designs and studies children’s play spaces, I worry about what could happen if schools continue to reduce school recess because of staffing issues, budget cuts or prioritization of students’ preparation for high-stakes tests focused solely on literacy and numeracy.</p>

<p>Research shows that this trend of not prioritizing recess could have significant effects on children’s and adolescents’ mental health, cognitive development and overall enjoyment of school.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770113/original/file-20261104-64-42z4rr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A group of teenagers are seen sitting together on benches outside of a red brick building." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770113/original/file-20261104-64-42z4rr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770113/original/file-20261104-64-42z4rr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770113/original/file-20261104-64-42z4rr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770113/original/file-20261104-64-42z4rr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770113/original/file-20261104-64-42z4rr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770113/original/file-20261104-64-42z4rr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770113/original/file-20261104-64-42z4rr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Older children and teenagers also benefit from getting regular breaks from the academics of a school day.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/multiracial-male-and-female-friends-sitting-in-royalty-free-image/1439953643?phrase=Recess%20teenagers%20school&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Maskot/Digital Vision via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>School are well intended but under strain</h2>

<p>The decline in time for recess comes at a moment when many schools and districts are under increasing pressure as a result of <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/08/upshot/public-schools-enrollment-crisis.html">declining student enrollment</a>, pressure to <a href="https://nces.ed.gov/surveys/spp/results.asp">meet state learning standards</a> and <a href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/2026/05/28/schools-making-budget-cuts-and-layoffs-due-to-inflation-enrollment-declines/">budget cuts</a>.  </p>

<p>For some schools, reduced staffing and the costs of maintaining outdoor play equipment to meet safety requirements have made it difficult to offer school recess. </p>

<p>For other schools, an assumption that more time for instruction equals a higher-quality education may be driving decisions to minimize or eliminate time for unstructured play. </p>

<p>Another factor that influences recess is when schools deny students recess time as a form of punishment – a policy that some scholars and educators <a href="https://americanhealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2025-12/Model%20Legislation.pdf">are trying to block through legislation</a>. </p>

<p>As childhood health, social and cognitive research demonstrates, the amount of time school recess is given matters in children’s development as whole human beings. I believe it is up to schools, districts and parents to advocate for and ensure children’s right to protected school recess time every day.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294764/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
