body: President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at a news conference during the NATO Summit in Ankara, Turkey, on July 8, 2026. | Krisztian Bocsi/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: It’s a whole new world for President Donald Trump.  What’s happening? So far, surprisingly little: As we wrote yesterday, Trump has largely stayed quiet since his shellacking in Tuesday’s midterms ( ballroom tour aside), and that continued on Thursday.  With the days counting down until Democrats take control of Congress, though, there are signs that things could begin to shift in his administration.  What could happen? A Cabinet shakeup, whether that means firings, resignations, or something in between

It’s not unusual after any midterm, and especially not after a loss this seismic (Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld stepped down the day after the 2006 midterms amid voter anger about Iraq).  Whatever happens, though, might need to happen fairly soon: It’s always possible that Trump could skate by with acting secretaries (he’s previously said he’s a fan ), but if he wants to get replacements confirmed, he’ll likely need to do it in the final two months of the current Republican Senate majority.  Who’s eyeing the exits? Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , potentially — but for very different reasons.  In Rubio’s case, it would give him a chance to distance himself from a radioactively unpopular presidency ahead of a potential 2028 presidential run — particularly as Vice President JD Vance is stuck writing social media posts about why the Iran war was maybe a bad idea .  Hegseth, meanwhile, is one of the public faces of the war
Trump has — for now — denied any designs on replacing Hegseth, but the secretary faces the prospect of impeachment as soon as next week

He’s also reportedly interested in being appointed to a soon-to-be-vacant US Senate seat for Tennessee, which would provide him a convenient escape (though based on Tuesday’s results , he might be an underdog to win an election anywhere in America)

What’s the big picture? We don’t yet know anything for sure about what’s next, but the chatter is reflective of the new world Trump and his administration are facing: dismally unpopular, deprived of easy confirmation hearings and cover from Republicans in Congress, and facing an aggressive oversight agenda

And with that, it’s time to log off… Hi readers, here’s a very cool story about an atmospheric phenomenon I’d never heard of before — transient luminous events, a type of lightning occurring in the upper atmosphere
You can read all about them — and see them! — here with a gift link.  Have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

title: Midterm voters clearly wanted to make America nice again
excerpt: Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton speaks to reporters at a canvassing event in Kansas City, Kansas on October 31, 2026. | Jim Vondruska/Getty Images Thi
body: Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton speaks to reporters at a canvassing event in Kansas City, Kansas on October 31, 2026. | Jim Vondruska/Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day
As the dust from Tuesday’s elections continues to settle, Republicans are looking around their shrunken ranks and wondering precisely where they went wrong on this one
President Donald Trump, who’s been generally (and surprisingly) mellow about his party’s loss, said it was because he wasn’t on the ballot

Vice President JD Vance, who hopes to lead MAGA into its post-Trump future, squarely blamed the war in Iran.  Republican operatives, meanwhile, have pointed to the affordability crisis, the appearance of corruption, and a slate of uninspiring candidates

And observers outside the party are floating multiple theories of their own, from the rise of the Christian left to the newly (or renewedly) blued youth vote .  Multiple things can be true at once, of course — and, in this case, they plainly are

It’s hard to look at the more than 44,000 races that played out across the country Tuesday and come away with a single unified theory of Democrats’ blowout.  But if you wanted to try, why not go with a theory that will make you feel better about other people? My colleague Christian Paz surveyed the landscape and came away with the conclusion that voters finally turned on cruelty this election
Go a little deeper View Link Christian reports on politics and religion for Vox, and even before the midterms, he had some firsthand experience with the anti-cruelty camp

In October, he flew to Kansas to spend some time on the campaign trail with Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton , a Methodist megachurch pastor who ran on a platform of “radical love,” mercy and kindness.  Hamilton’s chances looked remote when he launched his campaign: Kansas hadn’t elected a Democratic senator in almost a century
But on the trail, Christian met a lot of people — including registered Republicans — who liked the generous, neighborly way that Hamilton talked about politics and morality
On Tuesday, Hamilton won his Senate seat by roughly 5 points

And he celebrated in a characteristically gracious manner: “I want us to model what it looks like when thoughtful people actually work together to solve problems,” he said, “instead of slinging mud at each other.” For much of American history, that would have been a fairly anodyne comment

But this isn’t much of American history: We’re living in the age of Trump and Vance.  Meanness, incivility, and outright cruelty have been the political mode for the past 10 years, not just in how lawmakers speak and campaign (with insults, curses, epithets, innuendos, and undisguised racial animus) but also in how they legislate (namely, by pursuing and celebrating policies that cause distress to their political opponents and marginalized groups).  The clearest, cruelest example of both is probably Trump’s mass deportation campaign , which has seen almost 1 million largely law-abiding people ejected from the US
As part of that campaign, the Trump administration also regularly mocks and humiliates its targets in social media posts
As Christian explains in a forthcoming article for Vox, however, the midterms suggest that many voters find this nastiness off-putting, even if they’re concerned about immigration

In Colorado, where roughly half of residents surveyed last year called illegal immigration a “very serious” problem, 55 percent of voters nevertheless rejected a measure that would have required law enforcement to coordinate with federal immigration agents.  Voters also swung hard against the GOP in places that saw ICE raids or stricter enforcement, including heavily Hispanic areas of Florida, Kansas, and Texas. “These are voters who were very supportive of securing the border, very supportive of Border Patrol. … But the cruelty of what ICE was doing, tearing apart families and communities, was just a bridge too far” for them, the Democratic strategist Lis Smith told Vox
Elsewhere, candidates like Hamilton, Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico, and Ohio Gov.-elect Amy Acton prevailed over opponents known for their morally dubious pasts or ugly attack ads

Does this mean we’ve entered a new political era? A world where the nice guys… do sometimes win?! The midterms weren’t all sunshine and drum circles, after all: Some bona-fide jerks were also elected.  “I do anticipate a more conciliatory tone from the new voices heading into Congress — but when the 2028 primary season starts, I wonder how much these calmer heads will prevail,” Christian told me. “And at least for the GOP, everyone I’ve talked to seems to hope a new page will turn and a calmer politics will be embodied by the right — but at least not until Trump leaves office.”  One link for later ➨ Life is too short to finish bad books
So…don’t do it! I wish I’d taken this advice before slogging through a creepy, underplotted historical romance for a book club I probably won’t even stick with

Other tips to help you read more , even in our era of boundless distractions: Experiment with different formats — print, ebooks, audio — and take breaks to help shore up your attention span.  Before you go… Did you know… that the original Pledge of Allegiance didn’t include the words “under God”? President Dwight D
Eisenhower made that little edit during the anti-communist fervor of the 1950s
Today’s trivia: Which planet takes 165 Earth years to orbit around the sun? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you which e-commerce site bars users from selling their souls
That would be eBay, which first confronted this thorny metaphysical problem more than 25 years ago .

title: Rahm Emanuel knows how congressional Democrats can keep winning
excerpt: Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel speaks at the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, Illinois, on October 8, 2026. | Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP via Getty Images Dem
body: Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel speaks at the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, Illinois, on October 8, 2026. | Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP via Getty Images Democrats had a better night than anyone expected on Tuesday, winning sweeping majorities in both the House and the Senate as voters turned away from President Donald Trump and the Republican Party
Now, they have to figure out how to govern and contend with two more years of Trump’s presidency — and gear up to hold onto their new majorities in 2028
It’s a familiar situation for the party: Two decades ago, voters unhappy with President George W
Bush and the Iraq War propelled Democrats to congressional majorities in the 2006 midterms
Two years later, President Barack Obama won his first term and Democrats won even more seats in the House and Senate
Rahm Emanuel — a former US ambassador to Japan, Chicago mayor, White House chief of staff, and member of Congress — was there to witness it
He led the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee in 2006 when it led the charge for a Democratic House majority, and helped steer that majority from 2007 to 2009 as Democratic caucus chair

On Wednesday, he spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about how Democrats should think about their midterms success, what they should — and shouldn’t — do with their new power in 2027, and what all of that means for 2028
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
You’ve been here before personally, way back in 2006
It was a different Congress, a different president, certainly a different time
But can you tell people who don’t remember what position you were in back then? In 2006, I was chairman of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and led the effort to take back the House
Nancy Pelosi became speaker and I became caucus chair
I also helped in the 2008 cycle, where we added another 20 seats
So Democrats were in around 254 seats when President Obama put his left hand on the Bible
You guys win control of the House and Senate, and then use that control to notch another win in 2008
What did you do? What was the play? Let’s pull back a little, take a wider lens
One, this is a repudiation of the Republicans, not a vindication of the Democrats
I always thought that we were going to have a blue wave
But what we do in 2027 will determine whether we have won
The voters voted for change, not a Democratic version of more of the same
You have a broad-based coalition where non-MAGA Republicans and independents are giving the Democrats a second look
Make the election transformational, not transactional
Power-wash all of Washington, all three branches
Ban stock trading, ban prediction market participation, mandatory blind trust, mandatory term limits and/or retirement age
And then what I call the Jared Kushner rule
No foreign money while in government and no foreign money two years after
Do the hearings, but produce a piece of legislation that acts on the hearings
Second, everything’s going up in price
The last time it went up, Nancy Pelosi was speaker
Third, repeal all these tariffs that are driving prices up
Everything I just told you, you’ll get bipartisan votes
And it puts Trump in a position: You sign it, we win; you veto it, we win
There’s obviously this tension between “legislate” and “investigate” right now
Based on last night, people want “legislate.” But a lot of the base wants justice
They want [Defense Secretary Pete] Hegseth out
Tell me how you think Democrats should balance the two

Where is the Venezuela oil money? Where is Jared Kushner’s secret account with the Qatari money and the Saudi money? And what was he doing for them for that price? I’m all for that, but that’s not change
I’m against impeachment because it’s one person and you won’t get it done

title: What the midterms mean for 2028
excerpt: US Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters during a midterm election night watch party on November 4, 2026, in Detroit. | Salwan Georges/Getty Images Welcom
body: US Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters during a midterm election night watch party on November 4, 2026, in Detroit. | Salwan Georges/Getty Images Welcome to The Midterms, Actually
Every week I’ll be writing about two things: one big idea or trend I see forming, and one thing I’m hearing from a voice on the ground
One big idea Tuesday night, in a midterm election for the ages, Democrats notched sweeping victories across the country
They took back both chambers of Congress, and possibly broke the spirit of a Republican Party that has been firmly in President Donald Trump’s grip for the last decade
Early race calls in Georgia and North Carolina
Surprise wins in Kansas, South Carolina, and (maybe) Mississippi? This was a bloodbath
And it was a vindication for pollsters who had been flagging signs of Republican underperformance all year

Most importantly, it was the clearest message the American public could send to Trump’s administration: This president, his priorities, and his war of choice in Iran are out of step with public opinion
Trump wasn’t on the ballot, but he repeatedly told people to vote like he was
Americans accepted the challenge and largely retired the GOP candidates functioning as his proxy
Thinking about our reporting on America, Actually , where we’ve been charting the path to America’s post-Trump future one episode at a time, here are five lessons I’m taking from the results
They apply to the coming legislative fights in Congress and to the 2028 presidential primary. 1
It really was a populist backlash Throughout the year, candidates from James Talarico to Abdul El-Sayed said this election wasn’t about right versus left, but top versus bottom
For two years, Republicans and their allies claimed Trump’s 2024 coalition was a firm realignment, a fundamental break from Democrats by working-class voters

Fast-forward to this week: The New York Times’ voter analysis shows every big demographic moved toward Democrats, including men (17-point swing, Latino voters (28-point swing), and Asian voters (17-point swing)
First, Trump flopped, breaking his promises to lower prices and avoid foreign conflicts, among other things
Second, Democrats refocused their message, especially after Zohran Mamdani’s 2025 mayoral win in New York City, on affordability and tangible economic concerns

That brought back voters they lost in 2024, and reinforced the multiracial coalition they needed to overcome Republican advantages: a GOP-leaning Senate map, heavily gerrymandered districts, and a massive spending edge driven by big donors

Issues that won: Affordability, anti-corruption, anti-data centers So how did Democrats drive the bottom-versus-top message? Universally, with affordability, and by highlighting the choices Republicans made to follow Trump into the political abyss
When we were at a Speedway in battleground state Pennsylvania, even Trump voters were frustrated with the price of gas
Everyone, and I mean everyone, could draw the line between the war in Iran and the cost at the pump
When Pennsylvania voters are talking about the Strait of Hormuz, that’s a problem
It’s also a clear sign the GOP plan to blame the 2026 economy on former President Joe Biden wasn’t working
Here’s what one voter said: “I blame the president because he indicated to us he’s gonna drop all these costs

I know it can’t happen overnight, but when is it gonna happen?… It’s outrageous.” Two other issues carried the populist mood: Corruption Democrats across the country began hammering Trump on corruption earlier this year, and there’s real evidence the message was potent
We heard it in Virginia, and candidates like Jon Ossoff and Talarico made it their calling card
It wasn’t just that Trump was for sale
It was that he and his family were profiting from big business while things got more unaffordable for you
Data centers The third ingredient in this populist stew
Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas, Senate candidate Annie Andrews in South Carolina, and House candidate Will Lawrence in Michigan made a data center moratorium central to their campaigns
Data center moratoriums went an astounding 43-1 when put directly in front of voters, a sign of just how unpopular the issue has become
And like affordability and corruption, the data center message was never about just one thing
Voters were mad about the secretive process
Anxious about what artificial intelligence means for the future of work
And particularly enraged that big technology seemed to be profiting at their expense

Issues that lost: The GOP culture war The GOP had a huge spending advantage this cycle, and so much of that money went into ads painting Democrats as extreme, particularly on social and cultural issues. “ Talafreako ” in Texas, who they portrayed as an effeminate vegan
The Hasan Piker obsession in Michigan and the openly anti-Muslim and bigoted ads and rhetoric there and in places like Minnesota as well
And repeated hammering of a tactic that worked for Trump in 2024: stoking panic about transgender rights or “biological males” in women’s sports
It flopped in 2026, and there’s no way around it
The spending spree didn’t just fail to pan out; they seem to have lit their money on fire, given how roundly Americans rejected the pitch

title: The midterms were a youth revolt
excerpt: Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters on the campus of the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, Michigan, on November 3, 2026. | Jeff
body: Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters on the campus of the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, Michigan, on November 3, 2026. | Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images One of the most consequential subplots of the 2026 elections is that young voters swung back toward Democrats — hard.  Early data shows that 66 percent of adults under 30 voted for a Democrat for the House of Representatives, compared to just 31 percent who voted for a Republican — a gap of 35 percentage points — according to an analysis of exit polls from the Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE) at Tufts University

That’s a stark shift from 2024, when young voters backed Democratic House candidates by only a 14-point margin (and the Democratic candidate for president, former Vice President Kamala Harris, by 4 points)
Prior to that, in 2022, voters under 30 supported them by 28 points, all according to CIRCLE

The stunning shift back toward Democrats wasn’t necessarily a surprise, given that Gen Z can’t afford the culture war Republicans were running on and are fed up with the rising cost of living, fearful about AI and the job market, horrified by actions taken by ICE agents, and worried about war abroad
But this week’s decisive results blew even those expectations out of the water

The fall 2026 Harvard IOP youth poll had Democrats outperforming Republicans by 37 points among young voters.    The results are the latest confirmation that Gen Z is a voting bloc that can be swung, one that neither party will be able to take for granted moving forward, which makes sense for a generation who rejects political labels and identifies as 56 percent independent , according to Gallup data from earlier this year
In fact, Gen Z is more independent than millennials when they were their age.  “I don’t look for anything different depending on the party

Lower prices, gas, like I just want a better quality of living and I expect that from both parties,” a 19-year-old man from New York told me in a focus group on Wednesday.  Zooming out (pun intended), this generation grew up moving at the speed of the internet, and they vote that way too.  Beyond the overall swing, though, there were a number of notable data points in the early analysis of Gen Z’s enthusiastic role in routing Republicans on Tuesday

Here’s what we learned about what young voters wanted from the midterms and where they might be headed next.  The vibe shift is real Much was made — probably too much — of Gen Z’s woke backlash, and the rise of manosphere podcasters and tradwife TikTokers in 2024 as Republicans made major gains with younger voters.  But the election was also the latest sign that these trends may be exhausted a bit in the Trump era, and that energy is moving toward outsider politicians on the other side, like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.  Exit polls found that 9 percent of 18- to 29-year-old voters in Tuesday’s midterm elections identified as “MAGA.” But a whopping 34 percent said they considered themselves a “democratic socialist.” Now that doesn’t mean they’re signing up for the DSA or memorizing quotes by Marx, but it does signal that they increasingly identify more with the left wing’s more active approach when it comes to addressing issues like health care and housing costs — and willingness to buck the status quo.  Now, of course, this is just a poll of the voters who showed up — and it’s possible young conservatives were especially reluctant to turn out this election, in part because they’d grown disillusioned with Republicans over issues like the Iran war, which is its own sign of the new mood

Fifty-three percent of voters ages 18–29 in exit polls said they previously voted for Harris, versus just 25 percent who said they voted for President Donald Trump (this fall’s Harvard IOP youth poll signaled that fewer non-MAGA conservative youth planned to vote)
And a whopping 82 percent of young voters said they disapproved of Trump’s performance
The gender gap isn’t really closing Much ado was made about the young men who propelled Trump’s 2024 campaign victory — supporting him by a 1-point margin
They too moved left last night, backing House Democrats by 35 points, according to CNN’s voter polls
But even after young men’s massive shift toward Democrats, the gender gap isn’t closing — in fact, it’s still 22 points wide
And young women are a huge part of the story, too.  Gen Z women backed House Dems by 57 points, according to CNN’s 2026 voter polls, which is a 34-point jump from 2024
Time and time again, Gen Z women continue to be some of Democrats’ most loyal supporters, in ways that can create some uncomfortable social and political divides within this age group
The candidates matter too But it wasn’t just dissatisfaction with the status quo that blue-pilled young people this week

Candidate quality matters too — and there are certain candidates who really outperformed with this voting bloc.  While the party succeeded across the board, Senate candidates like Jon Ossoff in Georgia and James Talarico in Texas put up huge numbers with young voters
Ossoff won voters under 30 by 72 points , and Talarico by 60, per CNN voter polls

Both understand how to reach young voters online and in person, and talked about issues Gen Z cares about.    They’re also both millennials (Talarico is 37 and Ossoff is 39) — two of many in a slate of next-generation candidates generating headlines this week

Across the country, from Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel in Colorado, who’s 31, to Gov.-elect Rob Sand in Iowa, who’s 44, and Sen.-elect Annie Andrews in South Carolina, who’s 46, millennial and Xillennial candidates are having a moment.  A craving for civility Something pretty fascinating that surfaced in many of my recent Gen Z focus groups is an appetite among young people for candidates with “character.” They’ve only known politics to be hostile, toxic, and violent (they watched Charlie Kirk get assassinated on a college campus and saw Trump get shot a year prior) — and they’re ready to turn the page on that chapter.  “People are fatigued, especially with this administration’s alienation of certain groups and trying to spew hatred and fear
People are sick and tired of that,” a 22-year-old woman from Nevada told me last month

She pointed to Talarico’s campaign as refreshingly civil. “ When a candidate like Talarico comes in and has this campaign that’s centered around hope and similarity and unifying, that just seems so new and refreshing in this period.” Indeed, a big theme of the midterms in Texas and around the country was that Republican attacks focused on fear, culture war, and bullying — in Talarico’s case, his masculinity was attacked relentlessly — didn’t seem to help at all

And in many cases, these messages were specifically designed to fire up young men.  And a hunger for results There’s plenty of mysticism about Gen Z voters, but my research indicates they’re actually pretty practical
They’re looking for results, and we saw that manifest in how they voted this week
But the biggest mistake Democrats (and Republicans) could make is assuming that just because they shifted back left, they’re now Democrats
They are, perhaps, more up for grabs than ever before.  Above all else, young voters aren’t as complicated as everyone makes them out to be — they’re looking for results

And they moved away from Trump and the Republican Party in 2026 for the same reasons they supported him and his allies in the first place — frustration with the economy, a fear of war, and a rejection of the establishment which the president spent years railing against and now has come to represent.  This election’s first-time voters were just 8 years old when Trump was elected in 2016
Thirty-seven percent of 18- to 29-year-old voters who showed up to the polls were voting in their first midterms
They only know a political ecosystem dominated by this one man — and they’re ready for something different.

title: What Democrats could actually do to lower your healthcare costs
excerpt: Democrats’ massive wins on election night in Congress — and state races across the country — have opened the door for the party to deliver on one of its biggest
body: Democrats’ massive wins on election night in Congress — and state races across the country — have opened the door for the party to deliver on one of its biggest campaign promises: making people’s healthcare cheaper
When Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries declared victory on Tuesday night, he promised that his new majority would try to undo the massive Medicaid cuts that the GOP Congress approved in 2025

A new class of Democratic senators — including James Talarico in Texas, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, and Annie Andrews in South Carolina — are coming to Washington having backed a diverse suite of health policy ideas, from major overhauls like Medicare-for-all to targeted reforms like ending prior authorization for some services

Change doesn’t come easily, however, and people should keep their expectations in check: President Donald Trump is still in the White House, and that will limit how much policy work gets done in the next two years.  But that doesn’t mean we’re stuck, either
Everybody recognizes US healthcare is a mess, and lawmakers from both parties have expressed interest in smaller-scale changes that could actually pass in the next few years and get Trump’s signature

Given how massive the Democratic wins were, Republicans in Congress and even Trump himself may have a political incentive to cooperate with the new Democratic majorities: By a 19-point margin, voters said they trusted Democrats more than Republicans to address healthcare costs, according to a KFF analysis of exit poll data
And at the state level, Democrats will have freer rein to do what they want in the near term

Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF, said he expects Democrats to push through ambitious healthcare bills — such as a repeal of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s healthcare provisions — that Trump will veto. “Then the game of chess between Democrats and Trump will begin to figure out what on healthcare can actually get enacted,” he said
The other looming issue for Democrats will be the 2028 presidential campaign, in which candidates will have to figure out how much to promise if they win full control of the federal government
It could be a messy intra-party fight — or they could use this time to find a consensus that allows them to actually pass a bill in a few years

Will the progressive wing push hard for Medicare-for-all? Can Democrats unite around a public option? These questions won’t be answered definitively before 2029 — but whether Democrats can start to make headway in bridging their differences or not will go a long way toward determining what’s possible
There are a lot of balls in the air at once, even as Americans are desperate for relief right now
Here is how US healthcare could actually change at the federal and state level in the short term — and a look ahead at the long-term prospects for more far-reaching reforms
What Congress could do in the short term on healthcare Trump’s veto pen will dictate how far Democrats can go in the next two years
Both parties have serious criticisms of the health system, and, on some narrow problems, the two sides are actually pretty aligned on a need to do something
Those issues are the best bets for action in the next two years. 1) Reforms for Medicare payments One top target would be limited Medicare payment reforms

Medicare is the single biggest healthcare program in the US, and even smaller-scale changes could help reduce premiums and out-of-pocket costs for millions of American seniors, while saving taxpayers money
Here’s one opportunity for change : Under the current Medicare payment system, the price of a procedure is based in part on where the procedure is being done

So the cost of the exact same service could vary widely based simply on which building it’s performed in: A routine injection for knee pain or inflammation could cost $65 in a doctor’s office — but more than $300 if it’s done at a hospital’s outpatient clinic.  The reason for that huge discrepancy is that Medicare allows hospitals to charge a separate “facility fee” on top of the charge for the service itself

While the exact solution would need to be worked out by lawmakers, both sides have endorsed the idea of ensuring procedures cost the same no matter where they are performed.  That would be a win for patients, because their out-of-pocket costs are based on the total bill
And while the effect may not be enormous, lower hospital spending could also help soften premium hikes in the years to come for all Medicare enrollees
It’s a policy change that hospitals have long opposed, because they don’t want their payments cut
But DC insiders believe the appetite could be growing to do something about that and other narrow billing issues

Former Democratic healthcare adviser Ezekiel Emanuel and Trump healthcare ally Brian Blase co-authored a Washington Post op-ed endorsing a fix during the week leading up to the midterms. “Hospitals will always have their friends and allies,” Kim Monk, who tracks healthcare policy for the investment research firm Capital Alpha, said. “They’re the largest employers in a lot of districts

But I think there’s also a healthy amount of skepticism around, well, wait a minute…what are these billing practices ? I think it’s at least something that Congress is willing to take a look at.” And given how roundly voters rejected AI in the midterms, Democrats could also feel empowered to push for more transparency or even restrictions on how Medicare Advantage plans use AI in ways that lead to patients being denied coverage for medical services. 2) Fixing the No Surprises Act Of course, fixing healthcare is easier said than done — and sometimes well-intentioned policies don’t work
That’s why the next Congress could also look at remedying an earlier bill that aimed to address hospital billing but has gone awry in practice

The No Surprises Act passed in late 2020 (and was signed by Trump) to try to make sure that Americans didn’t get a massive bill if they were treated by an out-of-network provider when taken to a hospital for an emergency

But the arbitration process that the legislation had set up to figure out how much the hospital should be paid by the person’s insurer in that scenario has been a mess , with a huge backlog waiting to be cleared. “The No Surprises Act obviously is not working as intended

Maybe they can fix it,” Monk told me. “That’s another one we’re watching.” Insurers have blamed the law and its alleged favoritism toward providers in the arbitration process for contributing to recent premium hikes, and Democrats argue that creating a simpler system would help rein in rate increases for everyone. 3) Making medications cheaper Drug costs are a particular point of frustration for most Americans — and it’s another area where both Democrats and Republicans have been circling some of the same policy solutions

For instance, many Americans with diabetes still struggle to afford insulin , and there is one proposed solution in Congress that already has bipartisan support : a $35 cap for private health insurance plans, matching the cap that already exists in Medicare

Members from both parties have also co-sponsored bills making technical changes to prevent drug companies from using patent law to extend their monopolies and stave off generic competition, which could help bring cheaper versions of breakthrough drugs to the market sooner
One such bill passed the Senate unanimously over the summer, but was never taken up by the GOP-led House
Democrats could test Trump’s willingness to cut a healthcare deal by pushing legislation based on an idea he himself has endorsed: tying US drug prices to international averages
Democrats could also look to expand Medicare drug negotiations and make more medications eligible for cheaper prices

It’s in theory an issue where they could pick off some Republicans and even win over Trump, who has endorsed negotiations in the past. 4) Reversing the GOP’s Medicaid cuts One other unlikely change is still worth mentioning: Democrats are going to try to reverse the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s Medicaid cuts and restore lapsed funding for the ACA marketplaces
They have said that’s their top priority.  Trump probably isn’t going to sign a law repealing a big part of his own signature bill

But the new Democratic majorities are certainly going to press: DC insiders told me they expect Democrats to put together a healthcare-focused budget reconciliation package that can pass the Senate with only 50 votes and make overturning the Medicaid cuts its centerpiece.  This approach will allow them to make the case that they are trying to undo the damage that they accused Trump and the Republicans of inflicting throughout the 2026 campaign
It will force Republicans to take tough votes on an issue that has already cost them dearly at the ballot box

And it sets the stage to make a more serious run at overturning the OBBBA if Democrats win full control of the government in 2029. “That’s an opportunity for them to drive a wedge right into the Republicans,” Monk said. “Make Trump veto it

It becomes a 2028 issue.” What states could do on healthcare after the 2026 elections States have less sway than the federal government in shaping healthcare policy: They can’t touch Medicare, for example, nor the large employer plans that cover tens of millions of people

title: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
excerpt: Texas's data center boom may be over: Texas has been the fastest-growing data center market in the US, but a Democratic sweep of the governor's mansio
body: Texas's data center boom may be over: Texas has been the fastest-growing data center market in the US, but a Democratic sweep of the governor's mansion and Senate seat—with candidates who campaigned hard against data centers—has the industry bracing for moratoriums and permit freezes

The projects at stake are enormous: Two facilities alone—Stargate Frontier and Nexus Hubbard—represent thousands of megawatts of planned AI infrastructure, making any slowdown a serious blow to Big Tech's ambitions and the broader economy

Voters sent a clear message: Across the US, midterm voters backed efforts to shield ratepayers from data center-driven electricity costs and supported outright bans on new facilities—a sign that Big Tech has badly failed to convince the public that AI will actually improve their lives

Governing is harder than campaigning: Local officials, complicated county-by-county politics, and construction unions that backed Democratic candidates could all complicate any push for a sweeping moratorium. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148043" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts
But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position
Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton
Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott
At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years
Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail
Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing
At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September

That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself.  Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails
On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits
Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.  The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that
Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium
That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state
The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive

The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas

Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.  The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall
Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back
And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects
Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices
Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether

If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it

A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.  It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas
Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton
Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift

But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.  This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted

Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.  Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state
And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns

So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.

title: What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?
excerpt: Divided government limits big federal moves: Democrats now control both chambers of Congress, but without a two-thirds majority, Trump has the power to veto leg
body: Divided government limits big federal moves: Democrats now control both chambers of Congress, but without a two-thirds majority, Trump has the power to veto legislation—dramatically narrowing what's actually possible over the next two years

State and local wins could matter more: Democrats flipped Pennsylvania's government and Georgia's utility regulator, signaling real potential for renewable energy progress at the local level, even as Washington could stay gridlocked

Voters turned sharply against data centers: Of 41 local ballot measures on data center development, nearly all look poised to end in more restrictions. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148022" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night

And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramatic swing from Donald Trump’s victory two years ago.   While the results are striking, we probably won’t be seeing some of the big climate and energy policy shifts that have come in recent years as Congress and the presidency have changed hands
Instead, we’re entering a period of divided government, with a Congress that will likely do battle with Trump’s White House over the next two years

But even if the federal government isn’t likely to pass laws that overhaul energy and climate policy, the midterm results could be a big deal for energy, especially at the state and local level.  Let’s step back for just a moment to put these results in context
Readers might remember huge laws affecting climate and energy that were passed in just the last four years
The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included massive support for clean energy, including tax credits and government grants and loans
Then the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act essentially slashed much of the support and financial incentives in the IRA from two years before

What those two laws had in common was a period when the government was entirely united, with the Senate, House of Representatives, and presidency all controlled by the same party—the Democrats in the first case and the Republicans in the second
Now Democrats have captured a majority in both the Senate and the House
But Donald Trump is still in the White House
And crucially, neither chamber is anywhere close to a two-thirds Democratic majority
That’s the ratio that would be needed to override a presidential veto

So even if Congress puts together new legislation to boost climate measures and clean energy, Trump will need to sign it—and that dramatically narrows the scope of what might happen legislatively between now and the next election
There could be some bipartisan compromises
One interesting bit of legislation to watch immediately after the election is what happens with permitting reform
In late September, a bipartisan group of senators put forward a bill that would overhaul how new energy projects are reviewed and approved in the US
The law aims to cut red tape and speed up the permitting process
The Senate is set to vote on that package, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, on November 9, before the new Congress takes control in January
The White House has supported the bill, and it could pass the Senate if just a handful of Democrats join the Republican majority
But now, we might see Democrats wait until next year to try to renegotiate a deal, though anything would still need to pass muster with Trump
With Democratic control of Congress, we’ll likely see much more scrutiny of Trump and agencies controlled by his appointees
Democratic leaders have already signaled plans to go after leaders like EPA commissioner Lee Zeldin over cuts to staff and investments
Democrats will have the power to subpoena cabinet members and open investigations
Looking beyond the national results, a major trend to watch moving forward will be local action
Democrats swept local control of Pennsylvania, and officials there have signaled plans to support renewable energy and efforts to cut greenhouse-gas emissions
Democrats also took control of the Georgia Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years
The group regulates electric utilities, essentially controlling much of the grid’s buildout.  Among the broadest effects of these election results, though, will be for the data center industry
According to tracking from Ballotpedia, there were 41 local ballot questions related to data centers
And overwhelmingly, voters chose to restrict their development
Nearly every single one of these measures looks set to come down against data center development, as of the morning of November 4.  And AI critics fared well in their races, too
Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor’s seat in Texas, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott

During her campaign, Hinojosa called for a law to completely pause data center development; if passed, it could have major implications for both the state’s grid and the data center industry more broadly
We might not see dramatic new climate- or energy-related federal legislation between now and the next major US election
But many voters signaled, and quite loudly, that they wanted a change
We’ll see how much will shift in the next two years, and where that leaves us.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter

title: The Download: blended meat, restored sight, and the agentic web
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat  In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge served hungry students steaming marinara sauce and meatballs
The students loved them: 92% of those who tried them wanted them on the menu
Few could guess that mushrooms had been mixed into the meat
Dodge was testing a new product called 50/Cut from the company Joyn

The blend of seemingly simple ingredients—available as meatballs, burgers, and ground meat—could help solve one of the biggest challenges of the climate crisis: getting people to eat less meat, particularly beef
Joyn is among a wave of startups creating “blended meat,” which combines plant proteins with the real deal
The logic: The best meat replacement is … better meat

Get a taste of the startups betting on greener beef . —Meghan McCarron This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration More than 5 million people have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which retinal cells die off
Until now, no treatment could restore their vision
It combines a retinal implant with camera-equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision
After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients could read, do crosswords, and use their phones

Find out how the sight-restoring implant works . —Linda Marsa MIT Technology Review Narrated: The agentic web is here In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves
But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality
They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts
This new era is being called the agentic web, and it will inevitably transform the internet
Whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts
Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released

body: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991

body: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country
Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt
